things that have been of value and have given definition and sense of purpose to the term "Canadianism".
We on this side of the House are urging government members to reconsider Bill C-32, to understand the hurt out there and to begin to feel and share the hurt. If they feel it and begin to share it, they will not move on Bill C-32, because to feel it and share it would be to have a sense of compassion and a sense of duty.

Madam Speaker, I too would like to speak on the bill before the House. Bill C-32, would effectively cap the CAP for the three so-called wealthy provinces: Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
You may, Madam Speaker, being from a province which is not subject to this bill, say: "Well, that is fine. You are wealthy people in Alberta. You have no poor people there". I doubt that you would say that, but some people might think that. Therefore, one makes a sacrifice to try to balance the budget.
In starting, I would point out that on the weekend the Department of External Affairs has allegedly spent $140 million on a communications system that does not work.
You will have noticed, Madam Speaker, that last year the federal government spent $500 million on sending its public servants-one of whom I used to be-around the country. The government is spending about $160 billion a year now on some things which I think to most Canadians are simply beyond our means to afford.
I will spend time on this, although I realize I only have a few moments. I would like to talk a little bit about poverty in Alberta since a lot of people think it does not exist. There is a lot of poverty in Alberta. There is a lot of poverty in single families in my own constituency, and I have met a lot of them, invariably women because, as you know, divorce or separation, is instant povertization for women. In fact, one single parent told me recently that by her estimates, the husband's income actually goes up substantially when they separate, the wife's goes down enormously.
There is a great deal of poverty in Alberta and unfortunately it has been growing rapidly. There are 49,000 households in Alberta living below the poverty line. There is the working poor, which you know about as well. Children in Alberta are now marginally worse off than those of the average Canadian. I wonder how many
people outside of British Columbia and Alberta know that. It is actually higher for Alberta than it is nationally.
There are all kinds of indications which I think are irrefutable that poverty and the working poor children in Alberta are not living in the lap of luxury at all. What this bill does, as I am sure you know very well by now, Madam Speaker, is it is going to make it harder for us to provide assistance. It is going to make it harder for us to provide education. It is going to make it harder for the people in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario to provide things which probably are part of the glue that holds Canada together.
If this government removes enough of the glue that holds us together, I fear enormously for the future of my country. You may say that they are only doing it to these three provinces. What are we going to do next year when they do it to Manitoba, or to Saskatchewan where the farm price is probably unprecedented in this century, including the Depression years. If they can do it to three provinces, they can do it to any province.
I would ask members of this House to urge the government to withdraw the bill, not to go ahead with it given the present economic situation, because it will weaken the ability of three provinces in this country with thousands and thousands of poor families, families who need educational assistance, families who need hospital assistance, to provide those services.
According to the government's estimates, the three affected provinces will lose $2.13 billion in federal transfers over the five-year period through to 1995-96. Provincial estimates are significantly higher.
Under CAP, as you know, Madam Speaker, the federal and provincial governments share equally in the costs of basic necessities such as food, shelter, clothing, utilities and household supplies to persons who so qualify. Services are provided for poor people and lower income people through CAP and include such things as dental care, essential living services for disabled persons, foster homes for abused children, safe housing for abused women, subsidized child care for low income families.
The cap on CAP, as it has been termed, has been extended by the Conservative government and, of course, as we know the court has now recently ruled that it can do that. As a result of that ruling, the government will seek repayment of CAP funds transferred to the three provinces, including $40 million to British Colum-
September 25, 1991

bia, $400 million to Ontario, and I am afraid I do not know how much for Alberta.
This party, I am proud to say, has consistently opposed the cap on CAP. We do not support the Conservative government's measures to transfer the burden of the national debt and federal deficit reductions on to the backs of poor Canadians, in this case the three provinces at issue.
I am delighted that so many speakers on this side of the House have got up to oppose this bill. I assume, Madam Speaker, you are going to hear shortly from a colleague from Sudbury who will do the same. I think it is a very sad day, as an Albertan and a western Canadian, when a government is going to bring in a measure that will do significant harm to our fellow citizens in the three provinces which have difficulty getting by at the end of the month.
I would put it to you, Madam Speaker, that the bill makes a mockery of the 1984 election pledge of the now Prime Minister that social programs are "a sacred trust". It also digs the grave for universality. I believe it could well turn out to be part of the-perhaps tombstone is too strong a word-end of medicare as some health experts argue. Anti-poverty groups have said that the poor will be left defenceless. The Native Council of Canada has called this bill and its earlier predecessor C-69 "a national disaster for people already living in Third World conditions."
The bill is unacceptable to my party and, I believe, it is unacceptable to the vast majority of Canadians and certainly the vast majority of people living in the three affected provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak to Bill C-32, which is a bill to extend the cap on CAP. CAP, in essence, is the Canada Assistance Program which is the bill that provides or matches moneys to provinces for a number of welfare and social programs which affect, by and large, seniors, children, women and those people who are unfortunate enough to no longer have a job, to no longer collect unemployment insurance and are really in desperate need of welfare. Of course, we do have a law that states that if a person
Government Orders
qualifies in the municipalities, they must pay them the money.
As you know, this creates a tremendous burden on municipalities and so the property taxes end up being increased. In my community and in many communities in Ontario, already the property tax base is very high. People have been taxed to death and it continues to happen.
I must say something. It seems very strange to me to be standing here in this House, in essence speaking for the people of Ontario, defending the people of Ontario and speaking for the NDP government in Ontario, saying that we all know it has a huge deficit and this will certainly increase its deficit, but I wonder, over the last little while, why I have not heard any of my colleagues from the NDP rise and deliver any kind of speech on this subject. It seems rather passing strange to me that I, as a Liberal, am here defending the position of Bob Rae's NDP government in Ontario when I know that he has many colleagues here who do not seem to be standing up to speak on this subject.
Nevertheless, I feel very strongly about the issue. I feel that someone has to stand up and speak for those who have a veiy difficult time defending themselves in our social system.
I do agree with deficit reduction and with controlling the amounts of moneys that are spent. I find that very commendable, but I often wonder how a government can, on the one hand, say we are going to control the deficit and we are going to control it on the backs of those who have nothing, and then turn around and have money for many of the projects that please them and their friends. We have any amounts of moneys for computer programs and computer systems. We had one just the other day that we heard about in External Affairs. It was scheduled to cost $28 million and it is costing $148 million. There was money for that. There will be money, I am sure, for many other projects which happen to appeal to the Conservative government's friends.
It surprises me that suddenly there is no money to match for those provinces that are seemingly the richer provinces, although I would beg to differ now after what has been happening in Ontario with the massive longterm loss of jobs in the industrial sector.

Government Orders
This is not like the last recession in the 1980s. If you can recall in the early 1980s, we did have a very terrible recession in the country. It was very much a world-wide recession.
In the early 1980s, the jobs were put on hold. They did not disappear forever. These jobs are gone now. It seems to me that we have to give some consideration to the burden that will fall on the provinces and on the municipalities because obviously the provincial government has no room in its budget to take up the slack of what this government is not going to give them. It has already overspent in many areas, so it is going to pass it on to municipalities and municipal taxpayers.
I was once an alderman and a regional councillor, and I can recall how terrible it was for us to keep raising taxes. The people of Sudbury pay just about the highest municipal taxes in the province of Ontario, and yet already the budget for welfare has surpassed anything that they predicted. Obviously, that money will have to come from somewhere.
It is not just the welfare rolls. It is the other areas, the seniors and the homes for seniors. Every day we read of some of these homes which are inadequately funded. I was reading just the other day of one home-I am not sure where it is-where the staff actually had to go out and do the laundry because there had been no laundry delivered. There was no money to make sure that they had clean linen.
Have we forgotten that we do have a duty to our seniors, to make sure that they are well cared for? We must not forget that we owe them a debt. They did many things for us, and now it is our turn to do for them.
We must also not forget those who will follow after us, that is, our children. You all know, of course, of the desperate need of many of our children. Many of our children live below the poverty line. They live in homes where the income is very low. They live in homes where there is only one parent. That parent may not have a job. That parent may be living on social assistance.
What happens to these children? What kind of hope can we give them? I am convinced that somewhere, somehow we have to start co-operating with all levels of government. It is not fair for one government to decree to another one. Somehow there has to be a mechanism put into place so that every level of government can sit down and say: "Listen, we have these problems. We do have the problem of the deficit and the debt. Yes, we acknowledge that."
We also have a problem with people who are unemployed and with people who are on social assistance. We have children. We have the middle income, ordinary taxpayer who is absolutely pushed to the limit. In any of the subdivisions where people have kept their homes to see their property tax base continually increase year after year, is there any wonder why there is a revolt?
Do we forget that it does not matter which pocket the dollar comes from, be it the right pocket or the left pocket? It is all from the same person.
I think there should be some way that we could sit down together. Let us not pass this bill, Bill C-32. Let us come back with some kind of project where all levels of government will work together to help all sectors. Perhaps we could come up with some answers.
I know it is not easy, but there are no easy answers. Obviously, this is not the answer that it should be. It is certainly not an easy answer.
I plead with the members on the other side of the House. I know there are many of them who are compassionate. They do not all believe that they should hurt people. I plead with them to please all sit together, work together and try to resolve some of these problems.
Slashing, cutting or decreeing do not help. They really do not help.
I on the other hand would be very happy to sit down with these people and say: "Yes, let us all tighten our belts, but let us not forget those who need our help also". There are many instances where we can ourselves cut back on our spending and help those who cannot help themselves.
I think it is horrendous that now in the 1980s it seems that wherever we go there are food lines and people who are hungry. It is national disaster in a country with the numbers of resources and with the standard of living that we have that we should have that kind of a disaster befall us.
I understand that it is not always easy to address these issues, but it is certainly a very worth-while one. I have to ask again whether our friends to the left will be prepared to stand up and defend the province of Ontario. In my riding, we have three provincial NDP members. I wonder what they think of this. I wonder if the people from their party here in the national capital are willing to stand up and speak to this point. I have not heard any of them. I gather perhaps a few have spoken to the issue.
September 25, 1991

Have they just walked away from the fate of our poor Canadians? I do not know.
I can understand the people from the Conservative Party not wanting to rise because they are ashamed. I would be ashamed too if I was doing that to those who have less than I have. I can sympathize. I would be ashamed also.
I am not ashamed.

speechtext:
The member across the way tells me he is not ashamed. I think he is an exception. Otherwise, why are they not standing up and defending their position and saying why they are going to do this to all of these poor people.
I want to thank you, Madam Speaker, for your patience, and I want to ask that you do everything in your power to convince this government to be fair and honourable with regard to our poorest.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to rise and speak on debate on Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. The Canada Assistance Plan is a program created back in 1966 to permit the federal government to enter into cost sharing agreements with provincial governments for the provision of social assistance and also social welfare services for Canadians in need.
What does this bill do? It reaffirms, I believe, the agenda this government has been pursuing for seven years now, which is to attack the fundamental social safety that this country had established over decades and at the same time to pursue financial debt and deficit reduction in a clearly unbalanced way which ignores the tremendous social debt and deficits we all face in this country. Good government requires a balanced pursuit of both economic opportunity and social justice.
The bill introduced under the name of the Minister of Finance implements a measure announced in the 1991 budget and will drain-and the federal government admits this-more than $2.2 billion in federal transfers to affected provinces over five years through 1995 and 1996.
The provinces, for their part-and we are talking about Ontario, Alberta and B.C.-expect the actual lost
Government Orders
dollars to be much higher. Regardless of the final figures the same people do suffer. The provinces affected by these restraint measures are home to about half of the poor families in Canada, and 54 per cent of all welfare recipients under CAP live in these provinces.
The result is that the majority of the most vulnerable people living in this country are very hard hit by this measure. Of course the impact of this bill must be added to a similar measure passed as part of the 1990 budget which cut the growth of the same CAP transfers through 1991 and 1992.
What is the federal government targeting for cuts with this measure? It is kind of a fly-by-night operation. Under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal and provincial governments share equally in the cost of basic necessities such as food, shelter, clothing, utilities and household supplies needed by those most needy in our society.
Only a Conservative could question these vital programs as luxuries or frivolous spending. That is the conclusion from Bill C-32. Under CAP, services are provided for children who are in care and are in need of protection due to abuse or neglect, mentally and physically disabled persons, also one parent families, the aged, the unemployed, families or individuals in crisis, low income workers, and battered women.
Do these sound like people with the luxury of tightening their belts as the Minister of Finance keeps telling us? CAP services include dental care, essential living services for disabled persons, foster homes for abused children, safe housing for abused women, and subsidized child care for low income families. Many Canadians agree with financial responsibility in government, but do these sound like programs where federal dollars are being squandered or wasted? Hardly, and I would expect most Canadians do agree.
The restraints in Bill C-32 are bad enough in their own right, but they also confirm once again to the whole country this government's approach of attacking the most vulnerable in our society. It reminds everyone that for those at the bottom of the income ladder Tory times

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
are indeed tough times. It tells those who today must look to government for a hand to get in line behind the government's crusade against the deficit. It also says, once again, that this government will pursue the deficit problem alone above all others.
As Canada enters the 1990s there are compelling reasons to fear for the survival of the nation's social safety net, and it is because of this government. Since 1984 the Conservative government has pursued a legislative and fiscal agenda that demonstrates an abrupt departure from traditional values and priorities in this country.
One example is the erosion of universality of children's benefits and senior citizens in the legislation to tax back family allowances and old age pensions. It is true, as one observer put it, that under the Conservatives the responsibility of social policy has seemingly shifted focus from the Department of National Health and Welfare to the Department of Finance, hardly the social conscience of the federal government.
We are only now discovering what it means to have left the economists and tax lawyers at Finance in charge of social policies.
This government's record in a relatively short seven years stands as a clear rejection of Canada's proud record in advancing the cause of social justice and of enhancing our social safety net as a symbol of caring society.
In looking back, 1940 brought the Unemployment Insurance Act; 1945, the universal family allowance; 1944, the National Housing Act; and 1941, Central Mortgage and Housing. These were all measures which took steps to decrease the gap between rich and poor in this country.
The 1950s extended social safety in this country. Income security provisions for the elderly and for the disabled were substantially revised. In 1956 legislation was passed to furnish 50 per cent of provincial social assistance payments and share in the cost of provincial hospital insurance programs.
The 1960s brought the Canada Pension Plan, the old age security guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Assistance Plan. Through the 1970s these programs delivered to Canadians the kind of society they wanted and they believed in. The early 1980s continued this trend with the Canadian Health Act reaffirming universal medical coverage and an end to provincial extra billing.
This was a record of the past that Canadians had spoken in favour of through past governments. And what
was the goal through all these developments? They enabled the country to bring together its collective resources to enhance the development of the individual man, woman, and child and the individual's opportunity to succeed in life through education, health, and home.
Who would argue today that those were not good steps for Canada and every Canadian? Yet this government appears to believe its greatest achievement has been in reversing this proud record, and often in sneaky, backhanded sorts of way, never through the front door and never as a policy choice put before the Canadian people in an election.
This government has seen fit since 1984 to attack Canada's achievement as a country, that of a balanced agenda between economic opportunity and social justice, an attack that continues with Bill C-32.
Canadians will all remember the regressive steps under this government. There were cuts to medicare and post-secondary education through the EPF restraint, the clawback of old age pensions and family allowance benefits, the removal of the interest income deductions from the income tax forms, a measure which so helps seniors. Also there were cuts to unemployment insurance programs that have affected every part of the country. Special fees on student loans make the burden of education even bigger. Deindexation of the child tax credits, abandonment of child care, not once but three times, cuts to housing programs, and the list goes on.
Bill C-32 is yet another in the long list of regressive steps this government has taken over the years in reducing social expenditures in the name of fiscal restraint and deficit reduction. But this bill is also a very important symbol of this government's short-sighted approach, an approach of ignoring many of the real social needs facing this country while blindly focusing on the deficit.
As ministers opposite were whisked off to work this morning in their fancy limousines, hundreds of thousands of Canadians got out of bed but no longer had jobs to go to. This government appears oblivious to the plight of the beggar on the street. It is oblivious to the families slipping below the poverty line. It has little feeling for the family that cannot adequately feed and clothe itself. It is demonstrating all of this in Bill C-32 because its aim is to limit the benefits to those in this country who need
September 25, 1991

help the most. Those hon. members know that that is true.
Deficit reduction is a top priority of this government. The Prime Minister says it, the last Minister of Finance said it, and the new Minister of Finance says it. What the government has not learned is that deficit reduction is not a social policy. You cannot substitute good, sound forward looking social policy for a policy of deficit reduction. Good government always requires a much more balanced approach.
The government has failed to learn that it has to consider, along with the country's economic and financial deficits, the tremendous social debt and deficits that we also face. One cannot ignore one in favour of the other, as this government has done. One cannot abandon ones social targets and social policy goals in order to accommodate some sort of blind, narrow-minded view that the deficit should be our strait-jacket. This government has made the mistake of not forging a balanced approach.
Deficit reduction alone is not going to answer many of the real needs that are facing this country: job training, education, research and development. Deficit reduction is not a policy that improves the skills of one member of our work force, nor does deficit reduction feed people waiting in line at various food banks. For these challenges you need other policies, strong social policies on things like child care, income balance with economic policies. If we are going to build a caring and compassionate Canada we need all of those.
Canadians might again be able to look to their national government as a true reflection of values that we share as a people, a more equitable society. More economic as well as social concerns are all part of our national agenda.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to speak to Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. The purpose of Bill C-32 is to amend legislation that caps amounts paid by the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan to provinces that do not receive equalization payments.
Government Orders
The government has set a ceiling of 5 per cent on transfers to these provinces for 1990-91 and 1991-92. Today, Bill C-32 will maintain the 5 per cent ceiling until 1994-95. These provinces, Madam Speaker, are Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.
In his speech on September 23, the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization) argued that this bill was important as part of the government's restraint program. According to the minister, spending restraint was necessary to put the country's fiscal house in order. However, we must not forget it was this government's poor economic policies that were responsible for the first made-in-Canada recession.
Although the government keeps saying the recession is over, there are daily indications that the opposite is true. Today, 600 jobs were lost in the riding of Sudbury, the riding of my hon. friend right next to me. So even if the minister says the recession is over, it is not, Madam Speaker. It is still a fact of our daily lives.
My point is that this recession, whose effects we experience daily, has heightened the need for the kind of services provided under the Canada Assistance Program. As you know, Madam Speaker, contributions to the plan help meet Canadians' most fundamental needs, including food and shelter as well as various forms of social assistance. In fact, the Minister of State for Finance said as much in his speech last Monday.
That is why I wonder how the minister can justify extending these ceilings when Canadians need this kind of support more than ever before. Canadians have been hard hit by the GST, by lay-offs and by the recession created by this government, and now that same government has decided to cap assistance to Canadians in three provinces. That's Tory logic for you!
The Minister of State continued his statement by saying that Bill C-32 is based on the same economic doctrine that the government has pursued since 1984. That worries me a lot, Madam Speaker. I remember that in 1984, the Prime Minister based his whole election campaign on the creation of jobs, jobs, jobs. Seven years later-and it must be pointed out, Madam Speaker, that throughout those seven years, we experienced economic growth as never before in Canada. Nevertheless, after

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
seven years and the tremendous economic growth of 1984, 1985, 1986 and 1987, we find ourselves with the same unemployment rate as in 1984 when the Prime Minister wanted to create jobs and more jobs, as he promised all Canadians-he would create jobs and give them prosperity.
But here we are in a recession made in Canada by this same government and payments to the provinces are being cut. Madam Speaker, during the summer, like many members, I used the break from Parliament to go door to door and visit my constituents. In my riding of Saint-Leonard, because the federal government had cut transfer payments to the provinces, the provinces cut transfer payments to the municipalities and the municipality of Saint-Leonard had to impose a garbage tax on all citizens, be they owners, tenants or business people. The people of Saint-Leonard got the bill just as I was going door to door. I can tell you that they were not happy; they were desperate. They told me, "Look, this has got to stop. Always taxes and more taxes."
When I tried to explain the situation to them, I understood one thing, Madam Speaker: It is all very well, and it would have been easy, to say to my constituent, "This is not my field. I am a federal representative and this is a municipal matter. Go and see your city councillors." But they knew very well where it was coming from. They said, "This started at the federal level. You cut at the federal level, the province cut funds to the municipalities, but it is always the same taxpayers who pay." On one hand, we increase taxes and on the other, we cut services. Therefore the citizens are desperate, Madam Speaker, and of course this cannot continue. They have really had enough.
Since we returned, Madam Speaker, we have had all sorts of debates on Montreal. There are 10,000 more unemployed in Montreal since 1986. Every day, something closes. How will we get out of this? If we cut public assistance at the same time that people need it more than ever, it definitely cannot help the situation. Things will get worse and that is why crime is rising and we have all the troubles we do today in our society. It is because the economic situation is so terrible, the burden is so heavy that the people are really desperate.
Madam Speaker, I know that my time is running out-we are in a ten-minute period-but before concluding, I would not want to forget to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal, who led this debate for us in the Official Opposition. I would like to congratulate her on the outstanding work she has done in the past few days.
And I hope that when the time comes to vote, government members will think of the poor, the sick and the homeless in their ridings who need these programs that support public assistance.
Madam Speaker, a fair and adequate social policy cannot be replaced with only deficit cutting. I agree that a more balanced solution must be found for the country's economic and social problems. The Canada Assistance Plan is the cornerstone of our social security regime. It is a last resort for many Canadians, whatever province they live in, because the problems are the same everywhere, Madam Speaker. All this bill accomplishes is the destruction of social security measures. That is the Conservatives' real agenda.

I would like to cite an article from the Winnipeg Sun in the month of August. The title says it very clearly: "Feds will make poverty worse. The poor will always be with us, but thanks to the Mulroney Tories, there will be more of them and they will be worse off". We cannot say more clearly what the situation is. That is where we are collectively as a people today. The government is leading the attack on the poor, and we hear Canadians say that they have no more.
I remember a young woman who came to see me in my office in the month of August. She said: "Well, Mr. Gagliano, it is nice for you to say that we should be proud of our countiy, should be proud of our Canada. How can I be proud of my country when it has been two years since I finished school and I cannot find a job? It is easy for you, you have a job, but I do not have a job".
Those are feelings we get from our constituents when we go back to our ridings. This is first day of the debate on national unity. In a room not far away from this House members of Parliament and senators are meeting to start the unity debate. I hope they will remember that if we want to keep this countiy together we need economic prosperity. We need economic and social policies that can keep Canadians hoping there will be better days; so that our young people can go to school
September 25, 1991

knowing that after they graduate they can get a job; so that our seniors and our poor people, whenever they are in need, can have a roof over their heads, can have food on the table to eat and adequate health care services to take care of them.

Madam Speaker, it distresses me very much to have to debate this particular bill, Bill C-32 today. It makes me so angry that this government which had called this country's social programs a sacred trust has brought forward Bill C-32 to the House, asking for our approval to its cap on CAP, the Canada Assistance Plan.
It says to me that this government is terribly out of touch with the people of this country. If there is one thing that we as politicians hear across this country day after day after day, it is that we are out of touch. I like to think that I am not out of touch with the people in my riding. I cannot understand how a government can be so insensitive and morally bankrupt to bring in such a bill as this legislation today.
The other day the minister, in presenting this bill to the House, said that he was putting the cap on CAP in order to get our debt under control. He said the cut funding would be used to support programs Canadians want. What Canadians? If this government had sat down and had told the people of Canada of its vision and ideas for the future of this country and talked about the different options, I do not believe there is one Canadian who would be willing to see individual Canadians suffer as they are today in this country through poverty and lack of assistance.
This bill proposes to continue the cutback of funding to the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, supposedly the three richest provinces in this country. Yet we have heard week after week and month after month how Ontario, my province, is suffering day after day with more industries closing, more bankruptcies and more and more people unemployed.
It has affected the citizens of my riding of Northumberland most severely. If members of the government have not heard in their own ridings how it impacts on
Government Orders
people individually, I would like to say a few words about how it is impacting on the people in my riding.
The government's lack of vision and support of a healthy economy in this country through various fiscal and monetary policies that are inappropriate has caused the constant growth of the unemployment rate in Northumberland.
In 1988 in my riding of Northumberland, unemployment rates did not rise above 5.9 per cent. In August 1989, the rate was 3.7 per cent. In 1990, the rate rose in August to 7.9 per cent. This year in August, the rate was 10 per cent, but what is more significant is that this represented a decline from earlier rates this year which were above 16 per cent.
My riding is suffering terribly. People are not even on the unemployment rolls any more because there are not jobs for them to go to after their unemployment insurance is exhausted. They are going on to the welfare rolls, the very programs that this Canada Assistance Program was put in place to assist.
The number of people who are receiving welfare in my riding has increased dramatically, a change from August 1989 when the offices providing social assistance had only about 200 cases, to August of this year when the number of cases approached 900.
Statistically, the curve for social assistance decreases in August in my riding, but this year the curve from January forward has shown a steady incline. There is great concern that we have not seen the end of this curve rising this year as more and more of the people who are presently on unemployment insurance are required to seek social assistance as their only way to survive.
The people who receive social assistance are also having to line up with their families at food banks and be cared for by volunteers in different programs across my riding of Northumberland.
The cap on CAP not only has a very direct impact on those who are poorest in our society, those who are most deserving and needy of the type of assistance provided by this program, but it also impacts upon those professional people who are working in agencies trying to provide services that are covered with funding from the CAP program.

September 25, 1991
Privilege
In addition to those professionals, it also affects the volunteers who are working many hours, compassionately trying to provide necessary services for those most in need in my riding.
At this time of year in communities across the riding of Northumberland, United Appeal programs are taking place. Those programs are not successful without the contributions of many volunteers. In the past, the government provided assistance to the programs that those volunteers are involved with was a spur. It helped our volunteers to go forward and to provide the many hours of work to the benefit of the poorest in our area. The same thing is true for communities across this country.
The cap on CAP affects several programs, and they have been outlined by other speakers before me. Just to recapitulate, the CAP program provides social assistance from persons in need including single parents. Single parents with children are judged in our society to be the very poorest of the poor in our communities. Social assistance helps to provide for our aged, for our disabled, for our unemployed as I have indicated, and those unsung heros, those people who are low income working people with children who just are not able to survive on minimum wages. The CAP provides care in homes for aged people. It provides child care facilities and it provides transition homes for battered women.
The decline in our economy has had a dramatic impact on children in my riding of Northumberland. In 1991, the number of child care cases rose by 88.4 per cent from the 1984 level; from 509 cases to 959. In the same period, the child abuse cases rose by 279 per cent.
If you talk to the police forces in my communities they will tell you that no, unlike in the cities where drug abuse and drug related crimes are on the rise, it is not such a large problem in my community, but the calls that are surging up in number and that cause the most difficulty are cases of family violence. They attribute, very directly, the increase in the cases of family violence to the difficulty that families are having with their personal economies, families that suddenly find themselves unemployed, unable to cope with the economic obligations they have, not just to themselves personally, but to their families as well.
It is recognized that of those Canadian citizens receiving social assistance or welfare in this country, 40 per cent of them are children. The cap on CAP will have a direct impact on the suffering of children in this country.
Our Prime Minister went to New York last year in September for a summit for children which tried to urge all countries around the world to ratify a convention for the rights of the child. Children have the right to live well. By well I mean they have the right to food, housing and clothing, the basic needs. The cap on CAP, this bill, will prevent many children from having those very basic rights which are theirs.
I cannot say more about how distressed I am that day after day I go home to my riding and hear of more individual cases of families whose plans have changed because of a declining economy. That our government feels that cutting back on our debt problem on the backs of the poor is the way to resolve problems, to my mind, is very faulty thinking. In fact, we create a snowball effect where the costs of poverty will only increase by allowing more people to lapse into even more severe poverty.
There is no way that I can support this Bill C-32. [Translation]

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON A RENEWED CANADA
speechtext:
As I walked down the halls of Parliament this afternoon, Madam Speaker, I noticed that the Joint Committee on the Constitution which was established pursuant to the order of reference made by House on June 19, 1991, was sitting. Upon checking the official parliamentary returns I found that the membership has yet to be appointed. Having made all the necessary arragements to represent the Bloc Quebecois on this Joint Committee, I was surprised that the committee be allowed to convene before its members have been appointed and their names published in the Debates of
September 25, 1991

this House, so that I could see if I can sit on the committee or if I have been excluded from it.
I raised the issue with the committee, but I was told that the membership list had been left with the table officers after the House adjourned last night, claiming that the House was not sitting at that time.
The order of reference just can't be read that way, because if you take the trouble of mentioning in the order of reference that the list of members can be tabled when the House is not sitting, that also means that it can be presented when it does and only during the hours the House is sitting for publication the next day. Otherwise, the order would just state: the clerk of the committee can file the list with the table officers at any time. It would not mention specifically what to do "if the House is not sitting at the time".
Therefore, I consider that from the moment that the House has been sitting be it only one hour on a given day, the government or the person responsible for the tabling of the list should have tabled it while the House was sitting. The government cannot surreptitiously file a document with the Clerk during silent hours and think that it will be good enough. I repeat, it would not make any sense if that were the case. Otherwise, the government is going to start filing all kinds of documents and wait until we have adjourned for the day at 8 p.m. to table them and expect that is going to be just fine.
That being said, as regards the way my privileges as a member of Parliament were breached, I cannot tell from reading the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons whether I have been appointed or excluded as a member of the Bloc Quebecois.
My second point is this. On the list tabled yesterday the names of 32 members of Parliament appear, while according to the order of reference there were to be 30 members. The Table can certainly make this list available to you, Madam Speaker.
We can see that the four last names at the bottom of the list, all from the New Democratic Party, are asterisked. The inference seems to be that it will be up to the whip of that party to decide who will be a replacement one day and an ordinary member the next and vice-versa and so on. I understand that it may be difficult for the NDP to designate members, but the problem is that members like that are bound to cost us a lot in travel expenses, such as hotel rooms outside of Ottawa, in Ottawa and across the country, and much more just
Privilege
because they have joined the committee as I do not know what.
So, for these two reasons, Madam Speaker, I maintain that the committee which is officially sitting today and hearing as we speak the minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, is sitting illegally. This committee made various decisions this afternoon. As a member of Parliament, I could not move or second anything, I could not call for a vote, I could do absolutely nothing, while I, as a member of this House, had at least as much right as anyone else to be there and take such action. So this committee, which among other things has decided to broadcast its proceedings and incur substantial expenses, is now sitting illegally.
That is why I speak to you this afternoon on one hour's notice, instead of doing so at three o'clock, the time usually reserved for questions of privilege. I ask you, Madam Speaker, given the illegal situation in which the joint committee is operating-and I would point out that I am surprised that I, an elected representative who has won an election, am refused the right to participate, but unelected senators are appointed. But that is another problem that we can talk about later, Madam Speaker.
So there are now 30 or 32 people, we do not know the exact number, sitting and pretending to act as a committee of this House, but doing so illegally, incurring expenses and sowing confusion everywhere among all Canadians and Quebecers.
Madam Speaker, I ask you to rule immediately on these two questions.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course I do not know exactly what happened in discussions between the three whips. I speak now as a parliamentarian. It isn't always easy. An agreement was reached last night. Now I am normally a very disciplined person who bows to decisions that are made to promote harmony in the House and enable committees to operate effectively. I don't argue. However, I must say I was surprised when I attended the committee session this afternoon. I am very fond of this committee. I was a member in 1972 and travelled across Canada in the process. I have chaired many parliamentary committees, so I think I am in a position to offer a few comments you may wish to consider.
I am very surprised to see that the poor clerk- We have no right to ask a clerk to choose. The clerk's position on a committee is neutral. The clerk is an officer of the House.

I will proceed from now on in English. I see that in the membership, attendance and voting lists coming from the committee's directorate.

-there are 10 senators. Then we get to the MPs. There are 18 members of the House of Commons, with no distinguisghing characteristics, and then I see four names marked with an asterisk. I know what this may mean, but I wish we were told officially what is going on.
Everyone knows that my respected Whip, who is aware of my interest in constitutional matters, knows that I am available. He knows that, and I am telling him now, in front of everybody. He may not appreciate my carrying on and on about this, but I want to say that I am available, and if Misses Ouellet, Allmand, Guarnieri and Duhamel are not available and he wants to consider me, I will be available. The Standing Orders provide that the Whip files with the clerk, and all the clerk is supposed to do is say: The Liberal Party Whip or the Conservative Party Whip or the NDP Whip asks that Mr. Mark Assad, who is also interested in the question since he has been a member of other committees, substitute for Mr. Ouellet or whomever. So the same rules for everyone. No exceptions, because in that case, next week I will ask my Whip, my House Leader, to list a series of names of Liberal members marked with an asterisk, and then we will see who is important and who is not so important.
I respected my party's decision. They selected six members. We know they cannot be available all the time, all year. So the Whip will decide who replaces whom, as appropriate, at least as far as disciplined people like me are concerned, who respect our institutions. And I want to repeat publicly that I will be available if he thinks it is appropriate, and even if he doesn't, there is no law against a member who has a keen interest in the matter to go and sit down and listen. That is what I am doing, that is what I will do, and I am sure my Whip will understand.
So we have a document that is rather unusual. Well, in concluding, I must say that as a senior member of Parliament, this is the first time in 27 years and some months that I ever saw anything like this happen. I would like to understand what is going on, but I don't want an answer immediately. Patience is one of my virtues. I would therefore urge the Chair to take this under
September 25, 1991

advisement and then report back to the House and let us know exactly what should be done.

The hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead gave the Chair an hour's notice and raised a question of privilege that has stimulated some most interesting debate and involved members on all sides of the House. He told me about this morning's Debates or Journals in which the list of members did not appear. He seems to want to accuse the government of tabling the list "on the sly", as he said. Furthermore, he asks me to rule quickly, now, to decide for or against someone now.

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
I understand his impatience, but I also think that he would allow me time to act a little more circumspectly, to take the time to recheck with the clerks the special order of June 18 or 19, which I do not have at hand, and to find out at what time the members of the committee were named, and then determine what "when the House is sitting and when the House is not sitting" really means, a point he called into question just now.
