speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to add my voice to the cause of those on this side of the House who have taken serious issue with the government's introduction of Bill C-32, the bill laughably entitled an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan.
I say "laughably" as one might be referring to decapitation as a head cold.
Before I begin my remarks, however, I would like to express my concern for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. David Walker, who is currently under the weather in his hometown of Winnipeg. I realize that it is not the custom of this House to refer to the absence of a member, but I should like to make an exception in this case. The member for Winnipeg North Centre has been a strong, thoughtful opponent of this legislation and I will be hard pressed to do him justice today. I wish him a speedy recovery.
In the absence of the aforementioned hon. member, I am pleased that so many members of our caucus have risen to speak against Bill C-32. My colleagues have been quick to point out the obvious inequities which are contained in this bill.
I note that yesterday and the day before, no fewer than 20 members of my caucus have risen to voice their concerns and their dismay with this government. I am, therefore, glad to have an opportunity to make my own comments today on behalf of my constituents in Cape Breton Highlands-Canso.
What I believe we have before us today is a classic example of the government attempting to close the barn door after the horse has escaped. It goes beyond this, however. It is far more insidious. We have a government which is trying to shift the burden of the national debt for which it is primarily responsible on to the backs of provincial and municipal governments. It is a loathsome example of buck passing, and it is the Canadians who are least able who will ultimately pay the price.
Informed members of the media have questioned the motivation for this and similar acts coming from this government. They have suggested that this is part of an over-all electoral strategy on the part of the government to project itself as fiscally responsible. It is becoming abundantly clear to more and more Canadians that fiscally responsible is the last adjective one would use to describe this government's dismal economic record.
This is the government which inherited a public debt of $167 billion in 1984 and which has managed in seven short years to balloon this debt to over $400 billion today. This is a government which took on a deficit of $16
September 25, 1991

billion per year in 1984 and which has raised that deficit to over $30 billion.
In light of this, how can the Minister of State for Finance claim as he did in this House on Monday that his government "has taken steps to reduce government spending so that we can live within our means".
What this government is trying to do is off-load the debt in the name of fiscal responsibility on to the backs of the provinces and the municipalities. In the case of Bill C-32, it has chosen to do that by cutting into some of the most critical areas of social assistance. In doing so, it has devoided itself of the tough decisions as to who will suffer as a result.
I need not remind members of this House that the Canada Assistance Plan was established under the government of the Right Hon. Lester Pearson in 1966.
It allowed the federal government to enter into cost sharing agreements with provincial governments for the provision of social assistance and welfare service to those Canadians most in need.
It is these same Canadians whom the government would today abandon so callously. Bill C-32 provides for the implementation of one of the more despicable measures of the 1991 federal budget, namely, the extension of the 5 per cent cap on the rate of growth in transfer payments under the Canada Assistance Plan from two years to five years.
The original cap in growth was introduced in the 1990 federal budget for those provinces not receiving equalization payments, namely, British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. There can be no denying that this cap and the extension of it will severely weaken the ability of the governments of those provinces to provide federal/pro-vincial cost sharing social assistance programs. The government estimates that the cost to the province of Ontario alone will be $1 billion per annum. Over-all, this cap will cost the affected provinces some $2,135 billion at a time when the Canadian economy is attempting to pull out of the recession brought on by this government.
We all know that the province of Ontario has been devastated by this recession, and by the consequences of other misguided policies of this government, the free trade agreement, which has prompted a flood of companies to move south to the United States, and the GST, which has accelerated the practice of cross-border shop-
Govemment Orders
ping and has affected businesses all along the Ontario- U.S. border.
We in Atlantic Canada are not immune to the consequences of a severely weakened Ontario economy because sooner or later, and generally somewhat after the worst effects of the recession in Ontario, we will experience the worst effects of the recession in Atlantic Canada. Already we are starting to feel that as our economy in eastern Nova Scotia sinks ever and ever deeper into recession.
Let us examine more closely those areas of social assistance that are most likely to be affected: subsidized housing for low income Canadians, foster homes for abused children, safe houses for abused women, essential living services for disabled Canadians.
Are these the Canadians who should be paying the burden of this government's fiscal mismanagement? I suggest not, Madam Speaker, not in Ontario, not in British Columbia, not anywhere.
These are just a few examples. Underlying each example is the common knowledge that the Canadians who will be most adversely affected are those Canadians who are the most defenceless, the poor, the sick, women and children. But come election time, you can be sure that members of this government will be trumpeting their interpretation of events, how they restored a sense of fiscal responsibility. Such empty words when you consider the human potential that has been lost, and the suffering inflicted as a result.
Yesterday in this House, the Prime Minister introduced his government's plan for renewing confederation. It was obvious that his government has learned, to the detriment of Canadians, that you cannot exclude people from the process without grave results. The government has now pledged an open process wherein proposed changes will be considered and acted upon. Yet this government, through the introduction of this bill, continues to exclude those Canadians who most desperately need our help. It has not learned from its experience with Meech Lake that to exclude people, either politically or economically, is to do a grave injustice to the history and to the culture of our nation.
The government has seen fit to include the protection of property rights in the Charter, yet it does not see the merit in protecting those who have no property, those most in need of help. This government has consistently

Government Orders
ignored the plight of disadvantaged Canadians, as it continues to do with Bill C-32.
In conclusion, I would say that the experiences of the past suggest that if the government does not reform its way in this regard, in this most crucial of areas, it risks not only the lives of our least advantaged citizens. It risks the very nation itself.

Mr. Speaker, the government today with this bill is continuing its assault on the poorest and the most disadvantaged people in Canada. This thrust is not new.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the first measure taken by this government, after it assumed office in 1984, in the realm of social policies was to try to deindex the pensions of Canada's seniors. Seniors revolted en masse. They appeared on the Hill. Finally, the government had to back down. Had those seniors not had the will or the means to fight back, we in this House alone as members of Parliament would not have had the strength to make it happen. It was their demonstration of political will which forced this government to back down.
What do the Conservatives do? They continue their assault. They went about clawing back seniors' pensions and they were able to get that through. The heart had been taken out of many of the seniors who protested.
That assault continues today with their measure to take away the Canada Assistance Plan. This Canada Assistance Plan, as has been explained by my colleagues, is the last resort for those who suffer from poverty. When a person can get no assistance elsewhere, they have to resort to the social programs that come under the Canada Assistance Plan.
This was a plan entered into whereby the federal government said to the provinces: "We will bear half the cost of your ultimate social assistance programs". What has it done? It put a cap on it of 5 per cent a year for Ontario. This cap was put on at a particular time in our economic history. It was put on in June 1990 when unemployment in Ontario was at 5.8 per cent.
All of us are concerned about the deficit and our national debt. If we can find ways to economize, we want to do it. Maybe back in June 1990 there was some
justification, although I disagreed with it vehemently at that time because it was a program for the most needy in our society. There was maybe some justification when Ontario had only 5.8 per cent unemployment to cut back on the CAP program.
It did not take the Conservatives very long to come forward with another program. Eight months later, in February 1991, they said not only will this 5 per cent ceiling exist for two years, but they brought in a budget that said it is going to go for five years. This capping of the CAP is taking $2,135 billion away from the poor people of Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.
When they brought in that extending bill in the budget of February 1991, unemployment was no longer 5.8 per cent in Ontario. It was 9.5 per cent. Today, unemployment in Ontario is still slightly below our national average, but it is up to 9.9 per cent.
Even if you can say that the justification was that they had to save funds and they were going to impose that onus on the rich provinces, such as Ontario, back in 1990 that justification no longer existed. In February 1991 when they brought in the budget, or today when we are asked to vote on this bill, unemployment is high in Ontario.
In June 1990, when they brought this bill in originally, unemployment in Toronto was 4.5 per cent. Today it is above the national average. It is a disgrace that Canada's foremost city has unemployment of 10.8 per cent. What does this mean in terms of the poor of my city, the metropolitan Toronto area? What does this mean to the poor in Ontario?
Not only is unemployment dramatically up from when they brought in this bill, but welfare has risen incredibly. Welfare is up in the province of Ontario 64 per cent over a year ago, and yet the CAP program is going to cut it off at a 5 per cent increase. It has absolutely no relation to the needs of the people.
Maybe under some neo-Conservative philosophy this would be justified, if these people had alternatives. Maybe some neo-Conservative is going to say: "Let these people on welfare go out and get a job", but how can you find a job in the Toronto area when the unemployment is 10.8 per cent today? It is not their fault they are unemployed. It is this government, which has
September 25, 1991

brought in what is admitted to be a deliberately "made in Canada" recession; a recession it sparked in its monomaniacal attempt to deal with inflation. In the name of inflation, it went about taking us up to a record spread in interest rates above the U.S. rates. Never before in the history of Canada have Canadian interest rates been 5.8 per cent higher than American interest rates.
What did this do? It drove up our dollar. It drove up our dollar some 29 per cent from its low of a few years ago to its high today of over 88 cents.
The Tories say to us, as the Minister of Finance did the other day in this House, that isn't it a sign of confidence in our economy that our dollar is so strong. Mr. Speaker, it is absolute insanity.
The Liberal Party task force on deindustrialization travelled across this province for three months, starting in April. We listened to the people, the businesses-big businesses, small businesses-labour unions, experts, municipal councillors, the unemployed. We met with them in their town halls, their union halls, their closed down plants. The message was the same; this government gave us free trade, but at the same time it gave us free trade it took away our ability to compete. Our dollar went up some 20 per cent; it raised our interest rates; it has given us 32 tax increases so we cannot compete with the Americans in taxes. And then we have a government in Ontario that is threatening all sorts of other legislation, which means businesses will not come into Canada.
All of us on this side of the House hope that the recession is over, and there are a few signs that maybe things are getting better. But I was just talking with a major contractor who builds industrial buildings. I said: "How are you doing?" He said: "Well, I can hold on; I can hold on for maybe another year. It is just because I have a few buildings in the bank". He said: "But there are no new industrial construction projects going on". This is the story you are getting everywhere. Over the two and a half years since free trade came in, Canada has lost 261,000 or 13 per cent of all its manufacturing jobs. And, Mr. Speaker, with the recession, hopefully coming to an end, many of these jobs are not going to come back. They have moved to the United States and Mexico and with them have gone south the hopes of many young Canadians.
So here we have a government created policy of making a recession in Canada, a policy that anybody
Government Orders
could have told you-and we told you-was going to drive the jobs out of Canada. What are we doing to the people who are suffering the most, the people on welfare, the people whose unemployment insurance has expired, the people who want jobs but cannot get them, the single parents, the disabled, the elderly?
What are we doing to help them? We are cutting payments available to them for welfare. Mr. Speaker, there are times in the life of a society when you have to stand up and say enough is enough, it is not fair, it is not right, it is not proper. Our society is going to be judged, not by the SkyDomes or the coliseums or the large buildings on Bay Street, or the ports and the docks. This is not the legacy we are passing on to our children. History will judge us on the way we treated our fellow human beings, the measure of compassion and caring. Did we, in their time of need, respond when we have the riches?
We will be remembered for the way we treated the weakest in our society, the people who do not have the means to rise up and rebel, the people who are not mobilized and organized, and can stand on Parliament Hill and rub the Prime Minister's face in what he is doing to them. We shall try in this House, but for these people what a pittance, the CAP program itself should not be enough. We should be investing in these people, giving them retraining and the capability to rise up and become active parts of our economy and our society.
It is that which we ask. What this government is doing is a shame to all of us as Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to take the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-32, which is an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. What this means is that the federal government will cut the Canada Assistance Plan payments to certain provinces, in this case, British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
This plan was brought into the House of Commons back in 1966. It gives the provinces the authority to enter into cost sharing arrangements with the federal government for the provision of social assistance and social services. The federal government pays 50 per cent of the costs that are approved under this plan.

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
We have had the Canada Assistance Plan for 25 years. Yes, there have been problems. There were times when the provinces have expressed their concerns about this plan. I think that on the whole, this plan has worked relatively well.
I know in my own province of Prince Edward Island it has been the means whereby my province has been able to provide many services that otherwise would not have been possible.
The proposed amendment to the Canada Assistance Plan that we have before us this afternoon means that the federal government will drain $2.2 billion in federal transfers from the provinces affected, British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. That is a lot of money, $2.2 billion over a five-year period.
I want to give you a brief outline as to what this money is spent on. Children who are in care, and need protection due to abuse or neglect, mentally and physically disabled persons, one-parent families, the aged, the unemployed, families or individuals in crisis, low income workers, battered women.
Those are just a few examples of what the funding that comes from the federal government to the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan is used for. I know that the legislation we have before us today, Bill C-32, really does not pertain to the Atlantic area.
My concern is about the future and I have a real concern which I want to express this afternoon. This government has shown that it is heartless enough to cut the funding for services in the area where 50 per cent of the disadvantaged live in this country. If it cuts the funding for that 50 per cent, what is to stop the federal government from going after the other 50 per cent outside these provinces.
Basically my concern is that if this government goes ahead with Bill C-32, and I imagine it will because it has the majority, it will mean that the federal government will have its foot in the door, setting what I think is a very dangerous precedent.
I know in my own province of Prince Edward Island that we receive approximately $30 million a year under the Canada Assistance Plan. As I said, the federal government pays roughly 50 per cent of the services that the province provides under this plan. This funding goes toward very essential services, services that are really
needed in the province. We have the homemaker service in Prince Edward Island which is a very popular program. It is one which means that the elderly are able to live in their own homes because of services provided by people that come into the home.
Many of the individuals who take advantage of that service are people who are 70, 80 or older. Most of them have spent many years living in that community. In rural areas-certainly my district is mainly rural-we generally lack facilities to serve the needs of the elderly. That is why the homemaker service is particularly important. It is important that these people are able to stay in their own homes, in their own familiar surroundings where a lot of their friends are living, in a community where they have made a tremendous contribution through their earlier years.
That is one program that is offered in my province because of the funding from the Canada Assistance Plan. It is a wonderful program and certainly one that the seniors wholeheartedly endorse.
There are many other programs that the province funds from money from the federal government under CAP. It runs the sheltered workshops for the mentally handicapped. It runs group homes for people requiring that assistance. It helps to sponsor community agencies that help with transportation for the disabled. In many cases if the disabled were not able to be transported by that agency they would probably have to stay at home. This way they are able to get out to various events, meetings, and various types of entertainment.
The money that the province of Prince Edward Island gets through CAP is spent on very essential services.
There are others such as counselling and foster homes for abused children.
Mr. Speaker, you just signalled that I only have two minutes left, so I do not have time to elaborate on all of the tremendous services my province is able to offer because of the Canada Assistance Plan.
Certainly, as a former minister of social services, I understand the increasing cost pressures these services place on the provincial budget. I also know the resolve of provinces such as Prince Edward Island to ensure that these services are adequately maintained.
September 25, 1991

When the federal government cuts back on CAP, as it is doing with the bill before us this afternoon, it places great financial pressure on the affected provinces at a time when most provinces are trying to practise fiscal restraint.
As I stated earlier, the Canada Assistance Plan is essential in my province of Prince Edward Island. I know that this legislation today does not affect the Atlantic area now but my concern is for the future. By passing this legislation-as I said, the government has a majority so no doubt it will pass-this government will demonstrate once again that it is willing to implement its fiscal policies on the backs of the disadvantaged.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan, if passed will put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan transfers to Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.
This government believes that these three provinces do not need federal equalization payments, but this government does not tell the public that over 50 per cent of all welfare recipients under the CAP shared programs live in these three provinces. Ontario alone will lose about $1 billion this year because of the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.
What happens when the transfer payments are reduced or cut? People suffer. This government says that Ontario is a have province. What does that mean? What do we have in this have province of Ontario?
We have raging unemployment. That is what we have in Ontario. We have massive numbers of plant closures, such as the plant closure in Swansea in my riding. We have people who have been employed all their adult lives who find that their unemployment benefits have run out and they still have no job. These are people in their mid-fifties. Some, who are 60, have to work because their companies have not provided adequate pensions for their retirement.
What do these people do? They go on welfare. It is either that or beg for food from food banks. How humiliating. How depressing. Two years ago, there were
36.000	welfare cases in metro Toronto. Last year, that figure jumped to 50,000 and this year there are almost
88.000	cases. This is what we have in a have province.
Recently, a Liberal task force held hearings across Ontario, including the major cities and small villages. I joined the task force when it held hearings in metropolitan Toronto. We heard presentations by Mr. Alan Tonks, chairman of the Metropolitan Toronto Corporation. We
Government Orders
heard a brief by Mayor Art Eggleton of the city of Toronto. These two gentlemen alone represent and serve over two million people. They serve more than many premiers serve. People do not realize that some of these cities have populations larger than many entire provinces. These two gentlemen are responsible for providing services to and caring for over two million people. Both of these gentlemen said, and I will never forget it, that the federal government has abandoned the big cities.
We heard in Question Period about how Montreal has been abandoned and about the economic woes of that city. The government has abandoned Windsor. We have been hearing about the prices and the unemployment there. It has abandoned Hamilton and the city of Toronto.
Here are some more startling statistics. There are
130.000	people in metropolitan Toronto who are currently collecting unemployment insurance benefits. Can this government give me assurances that when its claims are exhausted they will get jobs? I think not. They are going to go on social assistance. Does the Prime Minister still think that Ontario is a have province? Does he think that B.C. and Alberta are have provinces?
I recently asked my constituents some questions in a survey sent to every household in my riding. In the comments section my constituents said over and over again that every Canadian should be equal and that every province should be equal. They know that Bill C-69 was wrong. They know that this bill, Bill C-32, is wrong. This government is not treating all Canadians equally when the provinces are divided into have and have not provinces.
When one is very ill one should have equal access to hospital care. Where is the principle of universality that we cherished in this country for so long? It is the backbone of fairness in Canada, and this government is blatantly ignoring that fact.
Metro Toronto hired 350 new case workers for welfare last year and has been forced to hire 250 more this year. One of my constituents came to me recently and asked for a letter of reference from me. I have known him for about 15 years now and he had a very successful photography business. He came to me and said: "Mr. Flis, I have had to sell off all of my equipment and I need a letter of reference". I said: "You need a letter of reference to go on welfare?" "No", he said, "I want to work for welfare". The number of welfare offices and personnel is growing by leaps and bounds to serve these
88.000	welfare cases. I complimented him because rather

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
than go on the welfare rolls himself he applied to work in the welfare office to serve others.
The Conservative government hangs its hat on the Supreme Court ruling that the federal government does have the authority to unilaterally limit increases to the Canada Assistance Plan. However, the federal government has a moral obligation to assist provinces in providing services and care to those who need help the most: disabled persons, those requiring dental care, seniors who now are bedridden and require intensive care, foster homes for abused children, safe housing for abused women, subsidized child care for low income families, and the label low income families can be deceiving.
One of my constituents, a single mother, wrote to me recently and explained that she is a very fortunate person because she is earning $37,000 a year. She gave me a breakdown of what she pays for rent, what she pays for child care, and what she pays for other services. At the end of the month she has only $34 left to spend to take her children to a movie or wherever. She is seriously thinking whether it is worth getting up at six in the morning to do this day in and day out and she is contemplating whether she should go on welfare.
Well, if someone earning $37,000 is having difficulty, imagine the people getting an income of $15,000 or $20,000 a year.
My party recommended to this government how to take some of these people off welfare rolls, but the government will not listen. We agree in helping to reduce the deficit. We agree in bringing the public debt down. We have thousands of self-exiles in Canada who, while they were waiting for landed immigrant status, could not work. The government would not give them work permits to work. They wanted to work but this government felt it was more profitable to put them on welfare rather than give them work permits. Then they put a cap to reduce transfer payments to the provinces. The provinces passed that on to the cities like Toronto to pay welfare to these people. I cannot understand how
this government can say it is managing this country very well. It is no wonder with this kind of mismanagement that the welfare rolls in Toronto are growing by leaps and bounds. It is no wonder that students come to me who cannot afford to go to university this fall because these of cuts and putting caps on CAP.
I hope that everyone listening will lobby, will appeal, that this Bill C-32 be killed.

Mr. Speaker, I too am glad to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of my constituents of Winnipeg North, the Liberal Party, and my other colleagues in the Liberal caucus who would like to speak as well, but time does not permit. This is a very important bill entitled an act to Amend the Canada Assistance Plan. In fact, I wonder whether we can call this an act to amend Canada. There is really nothing left untouched by the Tory government, nothing which is holy.
Nothing is given back, only taken away. The Conservatives took away the trains and the CBC. They tax tobacco but use none of the revenue to help people quit smoking. They freeze transfer payments, endanger medicare and reduce funds available for student loans, then they take the loan money and tax students three cents for every dollar they receive.
This is a heartless government. And the thing that makes it most heartless is how little it cares care for the children of Canada. A cap on the Canada Assistance Plan cuts social programs. Who benefits from social programs? The people who have nothing, and many of the people who have nothing are children.
The welfare rolls are full of children. These kids often go to school with empty stomachs because their mothers cannot afford food. How can you concentrate on math and reading and reading when your stomach is empty? These children cannot learn with barriers like the ones the government is erecting for them.
The government professes to wanting a leaner machine where the excess is trimmed and the bottom line is cost-efficiency. Well, the bottom line for a hungry child is this.
September 25, 1991

His family is poor. His father was laid off. It is because of free trade, the plant manager said. His mom stays home to care for his little sister. They cannot afford day care. He goes to school hungry. He is small for his age, unhealthy, humiliated, and falling further and further behind in school. The other children tease him, call him names because of his old clothes. Is this the face of the leaner system? Does cost-cutting mean taking security away from a child and his parents?
Only 6 per cent of the federal deficit is attributed to social programs. Meanwhile the government can raise, according to the book The Quick and the Dead-Brian Mulroney, Big Business and the Seduction of Canada by Linda McQuaig, an additional $6.8 billion by closing off tax breaks.
Let me just say a word about this book written by Linda McQuaig, a leading journalist. This book is a shocking portrait of greed and ambition in the highest places and what it has done to the fate of the nation. Are we trying to amend, with this bill, Canada?
Why not close the tax breaks and stop taking food from the mouths of children? Is the government afraid it will become unpopular with the people it feels matter most, the rich company executives and their heirs? Are they the people who make up that 12 per cent still in the polls supporting this government? Are the other 88 per cent of Canadians in the middle class and the working poor? I imagine so.
No, the government could not risk jeopardizing its popularity by offending the wealthy and big business. Forget the small businesses of this country. Forget that most taxes in this country are paid by the middle class.
Once an author and philosopher, John Ruskin, said in his work Unto This Last, Essay iii:
Whereas it has long been known and declared that the poor have
no right to the property of the rich, I wish it also to be known and
declared that the rich have no right to the property of the poor.
Why does this government not leave the poor what they have, and try to improve the lot of the poor, instead of taking what little they have left?
For 1.5 million Canadians, they no longer think about the problems of income tax, and as likely, property tax is no longer a concern either. Why? Because the government took away their jobs and will probably take away
Government Orders
their homes as well through its strictly private marketplace, rules-of-the-jungle boardroom logic. They are unemployed and fearful about the future of their families. To be unemployed and poor in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia feels no different than being unemployed in any other province, including my province of Manitoba. Poor is poor.
And 54 per cent of these poor people live in the three aforementioned provinces to be affected by this bill. The government calls these provinces rich. Rich compared to what provinces? It is relative. Should every province's greatest aspiration be to have a deficit as well? I worry about the precedent it is setting for the other provinces later on, because this government has an obsession with deficit reduction.
I would just like to briefly call to the attention of the House that the Standing Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology in its report of January 1, 1991 on children and poverty, Toward a Better Future clearly states that it will invest in our poor children. We will reap fivefold more in 20 years if spending on the poor is not deficit spending but investment in the future of our country.
This is a finance bill, according to the government. At the briefing session held for the opposition, officers from the Department of Finance explained the purpose of the bill, the need for restraint and cautioned: "The government cannot be a good financial steward on behalf of Canadian taxpayers if such transfers were allowed to grow without any restraint".
Where was the briefing from the Department of National Health and Welfare, explaining how, on behalf of Canadians, the government was showing itself a good social steward by forcing this bill through the House? I did not see the minister of health stand to defend this bill. I wonder if he is ashamed of his government. I believe he should be.
He knows he has lashed the burden of the national debt on to the backs of the sick, the youth, the unemployed and the seniors of Canada. It is battered women, forsaken children and all the abused who have been harnessed with the debt. There is no security, no safety, in this place called Canada.
Making the poor pay the national debt has become the life force driving this government.

September 25, 1991
Business of the House
I would like to conclude by just recalling that on November 24, 1989, almost two years ago, this House of Commons unanimously passed a motion which read: "That this House express its concern for the more than one million Canadian children currently living in poverty and seek to achieve the goal of eliminating poverty among Canadian children by the year 2000."
I would also like to call to the attention of this House that in 1965, almost 26 years ago, in the Speech from the Throne, the Canada Assistance Plan was one of the five elements in a program designed to abolish poverty in Canada. What have we done today? There is a bill before us to abolish the very basic program that will abolish poverty in the country. That, I think, is the sensitivity of this government. Truly pachydermatous, Mr. Speaker. No social conscience at all. I wish this government would wake up and withdraw this bill.

Mr. Speaker,
I am sure that you have noticed, as some of my other colleagues have noticed, that over the course of this debate there has been nary an individual who has risen to speak in favour of this bill. It is probably because all of those who are following this debate, both inside and outside this House, must be impressed with the nature of the negative components of this bill.
We are all familiar with the government's stated claim that what it wants to do is address the national debt and the deficit and put the country back on an economic keel that is appropriate for the aspirations and the needs of all Canadians everywhere in this country.
Yet it comes forward with a piece of legislation like Bill C-32, which extends all the negative elements we saw in the last session with Bill C-69 where we put a cap on the Canada Assistance Program.
It highlights just a couple of points that are worth noting. Some of my colleagues from this side of the House, more particularly from my party, have been eloquent, articulate, precise and forceful in the arguments that point to the fact that this is a most unjust bill. It is unjust for a couple of reasons.
First, it indicates that the government is transferring its responsibility for the national debt and for the deficit on to the provinces, and through them on to citizens who are least capable of maintaining the responsibility for that debt.
Government Orders
All members of this House are already familiar with the fact that when this government came to power in 1984 the national debt was high at $170 billion, but today, after seven years of this government, after five years of unprecedented economic growth and wealth and prosperity in Canada, after those kinds of conditions, our national debt stands at well over $400 billion and is approaching $420 billion.
The government is now turning to provinces and residents of those provinces. The government's economic policies in this Parliament turned conditions around to the negative and the disadvantage of all citizens. The government has now decided that three provinces, in particular Alberta, British Columbia and my province of Ontario, must now bear the brunt and responsibility of the government's inefficiencies, inadequacies, incompetence and downright stupidity when it comes to economic policies and fiscal and monetary management in this Parliament.
They do not know what they are doing either.

We are looking at a bill that essentially says that citizens of this country, no matter where they live, used to be equal in the sense that they had the same opportunity of access to government services. They had the same standing before law and they could get the same quality of services for the taxes that each and every one of them equitably paid. Now these citizens from these three provinces are to be treated differently.
Citizenship now has gradations of quality. Citizenship can no longer bring to an individual the same level of services in one province as it will in another.
At one time yes, perhaps Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario might have enjoyed greater prosperity. Not so today, and thank you in large measure, in fact almost exclusively, to the government's policies. We have seen them. We have seen evidence. We have seen enumeration of documentation, of statistics from independent sources, business communities, labour communities, our own Statistics Canada, pointing to the destruction of manufacturing in Canada as a result of the free trade agreement, pointing to the weakening of the national government's ability to deliver programs thanks to the government's spending habits, none of them indicating for a moment a priority which should be working toward

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
national unity that the government talked about so eloquently over the course of the last two days in its Canada unity package.
How can unity be developed when it has already been decided that through legislation Canadians will be treated differently from one province to another? How can we address unity? How can we talk about responsibility when at the same time we propose a bill such as Bill C-32 that essentially denies the federal government's responsibility when this program was put forward to share equally with the provinces in the cost of basic necessities for all Canadians such as: food, shelter, clothing, utilities and household supplies.
That was a basic principle that is now being eroded with this bill. We already attacked it, aggressively so with Bill C-69 in the last session, and we are doing it more nefariously again with Bill C-32.
My colleagues have already pointed out to government members, who seem to close their ears and their eyes to these sorts of things, that with this bill the federal government will renege on $2,135 billion until 1995 that would normally go to those provinces.
If citizens from three provinces are to be denied what is theirs by law, what is theirs by virtue of their participation in this country, what are we doing to the value of Canadian citizenship? What are we doing to the confidence Canadians have in their politicians, their elected government, to ensure that what is provided for them is the appropriate net that guards them against the vagaries of the economies and the vagaries of a cyclical marketplace? Well, not very much.
The other point I wanted to raise is that as with the other government fiscal and economic policies, and I am being generous now, this one is either ill-timed or wrongly focused. What are we doing? We are asking this House to accept a reduction of moneys designed to provide services that are generally put in place for those least advantaged.
Who are the least advantaged? Some 54 per cent of all individuals who fall in that poorer category live in the provinces that are being attacked by this bill, 54 per cent who would otherwise require the kinds of services that are now going to be cut. Make no mistake about this,
what this bill is doing is cutting services such as dental care, essential services for the disabled. It is providing fewer foster homes for abused children, less housing for abused women, and less housing for low income families.
Where is that going to hurt most? You heard my colleague from Willowdale talk about the plight of Ontario manufacturing. Ontario, which used to be a have province, is being reduced to a have not province thanks to the government side. I see a couple of the members and parliamentary secretaries beating their chests, taking credit for the devastation that is being wreaked on Ontario. I think that is shameful, especially shameful because this cap on CAP represents an additional increase in taxes. Who is being asked to pay more? In Ontario alone this bill might represent an additional reduction that will cost Ontario taxpayers an additional $1 billion in this coming year. That works out to about $112 per person or roughly $450 for the average family. Look at the increase in taxation. For those who are lucky enough to have a job, that comes on top of the 25 per cent increase in unemployment insurance last year and an additional 35 per cent in unemployment insurance premiums this year. The fact of the matter is that those who were able to bear the burden of taxation are no longer in such a condition.
We see, for example, and I regret to say this very much, in my own city of Toronto welfare cases have increased by 73 per cent from July 1990 to July 1991. There is an anticipation that it will increase to 250,000 over the course of this coming year. When we are talking about people who are in need, we need not go any further than look at Toronto. The unemployment rate is the highest of major cities. It has doubled since last year, 10.8 per cent this summer; over 226,000 people on unemployment rolls, thanks to this government's economic policies.
They are going to ask these same people to pay more. Where will they turn when their unemployment runs out? To welfare cases again.
I know you are asking me to stop, Mr. Speaker. Let me leave you with these terrible thoughts that should encourage everyone in this House to vote against this bill. In my own riding there are only 20 per cent of the factories still operating. We have lost the manufacturing
September 25, 1991

sector and we have 85 per cent unemployment in construction.
What we need is a government that gets its priorities straight, focuses its financial responsibilities appropriately and asks those who can pay to pay.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to spend some time in the House this evening talking about this ridiculous bill that the government is going to ram-jam down the throats of this House and the throats of Canadians, Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan.
I just want to take a couple of minutes to explain to people what the Canada Assistance Plan is and then I am sure it will become very clear in their minds the false results and the foolishness that the government is carrying on in cutting back on this funding.
The Canada Assistance Plan is a program that assists those less fortunate in Canada to have some of the services that we in Canada are proud to say that up until now we have been able to provide for that unfortunate sector of our society. The program assists provinces on a fifty-fifty basis, up until this bill is concluded by this majority government, for the funding of many of those services.
The Liberals have always opposed the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, as it is referred to, the cap on CAP. I can tell you that the Liberals will continue to oppose that, because it is not what we in the Liberal Party stand for.
What is happening is the government again is transferring the debt of this country over on to the backs of those who can least pay. I know they say it has been challenged in court. We all know that the British Columbia government challenged it and at the provincial level it won. But the federal government took it further than that and it went to the Supreme Court. At that stage the federal government won.
We can say therefore that what is being done is legally correct. I ask Canadians: Is it morally correct?
Absolutely not.

My colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence says: "Absolutely not". It is not morally correct.
We brag in Canada about treating all Canadians equally. What is happening with this bill now is back in the 1990 budget the government said that it was going to
Government Orders
cap it, that the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario were going to get increased funding up to 5 per cent above the previous year but, if there were anything required above that, too bad, those three provinces would not receive anything above 5 per cent. In the other provinces in Canada, if the requirement was there, they would live up to the moral expectation and moral responsibility of the federal government to do that. However, for those three particular provinces there is a cap at 5 per cent.
That's an increase.

Yes, that is an increase. No question that is an increase but it is not a fair increase to the province of Ontario, the province that I come from, for example- and I will refer to that for a moment-along with others. Ontario has been totally devastated in the last couple of years by hundreds of thousands of jobs leaving our province and hundreds of thousands more people going on social benefits and requiring social packages. That is all because of the actions of this government.
However, there is no ceiling for the other provinces. We as parliamentarians owe it to the other seven provinces to give them a warning that this government now has its toe in the door. Yes, the government has done it legally. It is legally correct, but it is not morally correct. I want to point that out.
Fifty-four per cent of the people in this country who require those social services are in the three very provinces in which the government is capping the increases-54 per cent.
One of the jobs, duties, and obligations of a central government is to collect the wealth from throughout the country and share and distribute it equally throughout the country, or as equally as it possibly can be done. I also point out to this House and to the members opposite that it is not only their duty to do that across the country but a duty and obligation to do that within each province as well. The government is certainly shirking its duty and responsibility.
This money provides such essential services to the poor and low income people as providing and assisting them with dental care, essential living services for disabled people, foster homes for abused children, safe houses for abused women, and subsidized child care for low income families. This is the type of assistance to Canadians that this government is reneging on and is

Government Orders
backing away from. Again I repeat it is shirking its responsibility.
It began on this course in the 1990 budget and said it was going to cap it for two years. Then along came the 1991 budget and the government extended that period. Now it is going continue it until 1995. Take warning, the rest of the provinces in Canada, your time will come. The Tories will do it to you as well. The toe is in the door.
I just want to give few figures before I wind up, to show how this is affecting my riding of Prince Edward-Hastings. I talked to some of the people in Hastings County, in particular, as recently as today and asked: "What is happening? Do we have an increased need for this?" Here are the figures. The increase in welfare rolls in Hastings County from August 1990 to August 1991 was 58 per cent. If we go back one more year prior to that, from August 1989 to August 1991, there was a 91 per cent increase. In the County of Hastings alone, compared to the large city of Toronto, it is not a lot in total numbers. Some 4.94 per cent of the people depend on social assistance for their existence. That is a total of 5,154 people.
The number of unemployment claimants in my area has risen 20 per cent from August 1990 to August 1991. With the changes this government saw fit in its lack of wisdom to put forward in Bill C-21, the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, we are seeing more and more people fall off the end of the UI rolls who have to be picked up by the social services roll. That adds to that cost.
We do not need that in Ontario. We do not need this in Canada, and we do not need it for our low income people. The government is being penny wise and pound foolish at a time when we should as a country and as a nation realize the importance of assisting these people, the important resource these people can be for our work force, our places of business and everything else. At a time when we should be investing in them, this government is divesting itself of these people and shirking its responsibility.
This is an absolutely foolish move on the part of the government. We will pay for this as a country, as a nation, and as time goes on.

Mr. Speaker, I stand here today to take part in this debate on Bill C-32. I think it is appropriate to discuss this legislation today right after the government tabled its proposals with regard to the Constitution of Canada. I believe this bill deals directly with the relations between the federal government and the provinces.

I am uncertain whether this bill is more iniquitous or more deceitful. It is definitely both, but I am not sure which one prevails.
It is iniquitous for many of the reasons my distinguished colleague from Prince Edward county said. It is a cut to those provinces-the three provinces of Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta-where more than 50 per cent of Canadians in need of social assistance live. It is a cut in real terms, in the sense that it is a limit on the amount of increase that will go to those provinces at a time when the economy, particularly in the province of Ontario, is very weak and has been weak from the beginning of the recession in the second quarter of 1990 until today.
Whether we are technically out of a recession is not the point. In Canada we say recessions start when the curve begins down and they end when the curve begins to go up. Even if a recovery has begun in the sense that the curve is beginning to go back up, we are still far from reaching the point on the curve we were at when the recession began.
We are going to continue to go through a period of time in which many Canadians are going to require social assistance. This is then a particularly iniquitous time to be cutting back on the payments to those provinces where the majority of needy people live.
What I am really unhappy about, as I said a moment ago in French, is that this bill comes at a time when all Canadians are debating some of the very important aspects of our federation. It comes at a time when the strain of keeping Canada together is weighing on all of us involved in public life, both at the federal and provincial levels.
This is a unilateral decision by the federal government to cut back on long established shared cost programs.

Shame.
September 25, 1991

It comes at a time when the need has never been greater partly because of the recession, which was described by the Conference Board of Canada as the first ever made-in-Canada recession and was brought on by the policies of the government opposite.
Nobody else had a recession.

My friend from Stratford says that nobody else had a recession. I quoted the Conference Board of Canada. It was not the Liberal Party that said this. Outside economic analysts say that this is the first time that a recession has actually been provoked in Canada by Canadian policies. I might add they were Canadian policies that were pursued particularly in 1989. Why did we have high interest rates in 1989? Because the government opposite pursued a policy in 1988 of attempting to buy an election when growth in Canada was about 5 per cent. It cut taxes. It permitted a much more open monetary policy and the result was high inflation in 1989 and high interest rates bringing on a recession in 1990. What did it do about it? It cut the payments to the provinces for social assistance by capping them at a 5 per cent increase.
Not only is the need brought on by the recession, but at the same time it brought in a program of unemployment insurance reforms which throughout Canada has resulted in many more people being in need of social assistance. Furthermore, it has pursued a completely hopeless policy in dealing with a large number of claimants for refugee status in Canada, which take people who have sought protection by being on our shores, and during the time that they await determination of their refugee status, are unable to work in Canada and therefore have to go on social assistance.
Who pays for that? It is paid for by the municipality with provincial support. As we know, as a result of this bill and Bill C-69 which preceded it last year, the support which was to come to the provinces from the federal government is being capped at 5 per cent, when the need is being generated by the federal government itself.
I think the official title of this bill is an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. It should be called the federal transfer of debt act. This is in effect an attempt to confuse the Canadian people into thinking that the government opposite is actually doing something about
Government Orders
its deficit and debt problem, when in reality what it is doing is transferring its debt to the provinces.
Then we have the disgraceful performance of the Prime Minister of Canada going overseas, washing our linen before investors in Japan, criticizing the Ontario government, whose policies with which I do not happen to agree, but upon whom the federal government has transferred $1 billion of debt this year alone through this particular cap on CAP.
What the province and the federal government need to do, and I do not think there should be any cause for disagreement about this, is sit down together and make sure that there is an agreement on design and delivery of social assistance. Give the federal government a role in designing these programs so that there is co-operation flowing both ways. Then lock in the commitment to help fund the programs as agreed.
What we have here is the provinces spending federal money, granted without control, without limit, but the federal government cutting back the funds without consultation. No wonder things are not working right.
The transfer of debt to the provinces is not the way to solve any one's debt problem. Last week, we had the Minister of Finance in this House blaming provincial government borrowing for keeping the Canadian dollar as high as it is. Excuse me, but if the federal government, through the cut in transfer payments for post-secondary education and health care and the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan payments is forcing provincial deficits up, how can the Minister of Finance stand up in this House and criticize the provincial governments for borrowing too much? That is why I suggest that this really is as deceitful as it is iniquitous.
This is not an easy time for federations around the world. Canada has an opportunity, by making our federal system work, to be an example for federations elsewhere. My suggestion to the government is this, that they back off this ridiculous plan, and that they go to the discussion table with the provinces and say: "We have a problem, not the federal government, not the provincial governments, but we Canadians have a problem.
Let's find a way to address that problem collectively and co-operatively. Let's find solutions to the issues that confront us; recession, a weak economy, poverty in our cities, crime in our cities and the fact that our biggest deficit in Canada is soon not going to be the financial

September 25, 1991
Government Orders
deficit which is big enough, but the deficit in wasted human lives and lost hope."

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill as I have risen to speak on many others in nearly three years as the member for Halifax. I begin my remarks with a sense of disappointment, almost a sense of depression and certainly a sense of gloom.
The Canada Assistance Plan should be one of those programs that applies in all Canadian jurisdictions at the same rate, in the same way and for the same benefit to those who are in need. To put a cap on CAP is to effectively say to three provinces: "The poor people in your province are not as poor as poor people in other provinces."
I am an Atlantic Canadian, which everyone knows. I am a Nova Scotian, which everyone knows. Since we made the collective decision 124 years ago to come into Confederation, a decision that we have never regretted and a decision that we are proud of, we have, as Nova Scotians, seen a steady decline in our prosperity.
There are a number of reasons for that. There are shifts in world economy, there are specific government programs that have worked against the interests of Atlantic Canada in favour of the centre of the country, but I am not going to get into those specifics. Suffice it to say that poverty is not an unknown factor in the Atlantic region of this country. Extreme poverty is sadly not an unknown factor. There are very few people who live in the four eastern provinces of this country who cannot describe poverty on a firsthand basis. Maybe they, themselves, have not been poor-lucky them-but they have seen it, they have worked with it and they have worked against it.
Perhaps it seems odd. In one sense, certain members of the government have tried to say that capping CAP in the so-called have provinces will somehow create more benefit in the have not provinces. That is not what Canada is about, and that is not what members from the other have not regions want. It is certainly not what our constituents want.
We believe in the universality of our social safety net. We believe that one of the sacred trusts, dare I use those words that have been so sadly soiled in the last few years, for the people of Canada is the whole issue of dignity in
social programs. To maintain the dignity of those people who must rely upon governments for help, the whole concept of universality is key.
If suddenly three provinces are held to a different standard, to a different amount of money on percentage bases and per capita bases, then that means there are different levels of Canadians. In this time of constitutional crisis, in this time of what we all pray will be constitutional and national renewal, this is something we do not need.
There are not different levels of Canadianism. There are not different levels of citizenship. There may well be different levels of talent and different levels of need and different levels of commitment, but when it comes to access to government services, one Canadian is supposed to be the same as another. To put a cap the CAP in three provinces is to give the lie to that statement.
What is it going to mean in actual practice in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario? It is going to mean that those provincial governments, faced with the cap over the next five years, are going to have to rob Peter to pay Paul. They are going to have to take from their own provincial coffers for programs that are desperately needed to cover off the need for social assistance.
While we are looking at what this particular pernicious piece of legislation does, we cannot look at it in a vacuum, because there are other things that are happening that are affecting provincial and municipal budgets in this country today that are a direct result of the policies of this government. I refer, of course, to the reforms, and I use that word in its loosest term, to the Unemployment Insurance Act that we saw rammed through in the last Parliament. No one in this Chamber will ever forget it.
What that has effectively done is disembowl the unemployment income insurance program in this country. It has driven people, who in the past, might have been able to tide themselves over through periods of unemployment, particularly in this recession which has seen the highest rate of bankruptcy in the history of this country, and particularly in a recession created in this country by the policies of this government. But that is
September 25, 1991

gone. Any kind of safety net from unemployment insurance is effectively out the window.
It is certainly out the window in my region and I know it is out the window in parts of northern and eastern Ontario, northern Canada generally, northern British Columbia and northern Alberta. It is certainly out the window in a lot of the major cities such as Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton and the major cities of Ontario. UI as we know it does not exist any more and all of us who sit in this Chamber are aware of it. Certainly those of us on this side of the House mourn its loss.
What does that do? That again puts extra pressure on hard pressed provincial governments and hard pressed provincial budgets. These governments had a right to expect some sort of stability from a federal government that claims to believe that all Canadians are equal.
We hear again that Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia are rich provinces. In Nova Scotia where I represent the people of Halifax, the poor people are no poorer in the long run than poor people in Toronto or the homeless in Vancouver or poor people in northern Ontario. Poor people are poor people and provincial governments are governments and there is only so much they can do. There is only so much that can be stretched to cover what is necessary for people to survive.
We did not even have time to touch on the whole concept of the dignity of people who need to think that emergency measures such as social assistance and unemployment insurance are there to hold them up and help them. Capping the CAP, like gutting unemployment insurance, is an assault on low income people across this country. It is an assault on provincial governments across this country. It is an assault on municipal governments across this country. It is the federal government standing up and saying: "The Canadian social safety net, the Canadian social contract exists no longer. We now live in a time where you sink or you swim and if you cannot swim, do not look to me for a life preserver, do not look to me for assistance."
This is not what Canada is about. This is not what we were elected and what my colleagues on the other side were elected to do here. This is not the Canadian way. It is not something that any of us can continue to stand for.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should amend the Public Service Superannuation Act so that any Public Service employee who has lost his or her job on or after January 1st, 1988, as a result of a Public Service downsizing programme, and who had reached fifty years of age and had to his or her credit not less than ten years of pensionable service, would be entitled to receive a pension reduced by the product obtained by multiplying: a) five per cent of the amount of the pension that would have been payable if the employee had been fifty-five years of age at the time of the loss of his or her job b) 55 minus the age of the employee at the time of the loss of his or her job.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to ask today that the amendments already submitted in motion M-385, which pertains to the Public Service Superannuation Act, be accepted.
The thrust of my motion is to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act in order to address the plight of people who lost their jobs due to downsizing.
At present, employees aged between 50 and 54 receive a considerably smaller pension than those who are facing the same situation, but who are 55 years old or over.

When an employee in the Public Service becomes redundant due to downsizing and that person is 55 years of age or over and he or she has been employed on a full-time basis in the Public Service for a minimum of 10 years, the Public Service Superannuation Act says: "If at the time he ceases to be so employed and he has reached 55 years of age, has been employed in the Public Service on a full-time basis for a period of or for periods totally

September 25, 1991
Private Members' Business
at least 10 years and does not voluntarily retire from the Public Service, an annual allowance payable immediately on his so ceasing to be employed equal to the amount of the deferred annuity referred to in clause (a), reduced by the product obtained by multiplying: (1) 5 per cent of the amount of that annuity, by (2) 30 minus the number of years to the nearest one-tenth of a year of the pensionable service to his credit".
In other words, if a person is between 60 and 65 and is laid off from the federal government, he or she receives a full pension. A laid off employee who is between the age of 55 and 60 receives a pension reduced by 25 per cent or what he or she would receive at 60 years of age.
The act continues with this statement: "except that in any such case the whole or any part of the reduction provided for by this clause may be waived by the Treasury Board".
It is my understanding that Treasury Board has used this waiver in some cases when the person affected was 55 years of age or over.
People who are laid off from the federal government see their pension reduced unless there is a waiver from the Treasury Board.

The reality of current government practices is that many people under the age of 55 are being laid off through no fault of their own. Statistics which were obtained by my office for the period January 1, 1990 to December 31, 1990 indicate that a total of 357 employees who had been appointed under the Public Service Employment Act to indeterminate and permanent positions lost their jobs in that calendar year. Of these, 60 were over the age of 55 and 31 were between the ages of 50 and 54. The other 266 employees were 49 years of age and under.

The riding I represent has no less than 10,000 people who declared, during the 1986 census, that they worked for the federal public service. This is one of the largest
concentration of civil servants in a given region of the country.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, people in my riding are going to be particularly affected by downsizing by contracting out, by relocation and other measures that the government chose to impose on its civil servants.

The case must be made here for those people 50 years of age and over. Unfortunately, society is not totally accepting of the re-employment of people in that age bracket. It is neither a pleasant nor a seemingly fair statement, but it is true.
Employment centres and private consulting firms, such as Casey and Associates Business Centres Limited, located in my riding, are faced with this reality each day. The owner, Femande Casey, at 53 years of age a senior executive with the federal government who had 28 years experience, was the victim of this outdated legislation. Her only recourse was to accept a reduced pension or engage legal counsel to try to waive the penalty to her pension. It cost her thousands of dollars, months of anguish and considerable personal suffering. She now assists and counsels numerous former public servants in coping with this economic impact. She is frequently bringing to my attention the harsh reality that many of her clients face. After dedicating one's adult years to the Public Service, the shock and reality of layoff and the uncertainty for re-employment is devastating for many of her clients.
Her challenge begins with building their confidence, and then finding employment. She is quick to point out that most of her clients are former public servants, 50 to 60 years of age, an age group that is not particularly attractive to many employers and with skills that are not easily transferred from the public to the private sector. Where does a former public servant who has specialized, say, in staffing or in preparing ministerial briefing notes look for employment in the private sector? Jobs are extremely difficult to come by in Canada's present economy for the young, let alone for the grey culture.
After dedicating ones adult years to the Public Service, what a shock it must be-I repeat, Mr. Speaker-what a shock it must be to arrive at work to the reality of a layoff and the uncertainty of re-employment.



September 25, 1991

In October 1990 I asked the President of the Treasury Board to provide me with statistics concerning people in the age 50 to 54 category who had lost their positions in the Public Service because of the government's downsizing policy. Treasury Board's answer to me was as follows: "Since February 1, 1990, 149 employees in the age category 50 to 54 have been laid off from the Public Service. Of this number, 36 have been reappointed to the Public Service.

Thirty-six people only succeeded in finding another job in the Public Service.
The private sector might have hired about the same number. So that leaves two-thirds of the employees out of jobs.

Should these laid off employees between the ages of 50 and 54 be forced to take their pension, they are dealt with in the Public Service Superannuation Act as follows: Section 13(l)(c)(2)(d) states that their annuity will be deemed as being the same as for those who are aged 55 and over, with a reduction of 5 per cent of the total amount of the pension for each year between the ages of 50 and 60.
What this amounts to is a further reduction of 25 per cent in benefits between those received by an employee who is laid off at 50 and one who is laid off at 55. Specifically, a laid off employee who is 55 has his or her pension reduced by 25 per cent for five years. One who is between 50 and 54 has his or her pension reduced a further 25 per cent, for a total reduction of 50 per cent.
All of these calculations take into consideration that each has at least 10 years of pensionable employment.

With my resolution, I want to try and correct this situation through amendments to the Act. Consequently, Parliament should recognize that an employee should not be subjected to actuarial reduction if he loses his job through no fault of his own. The Public Service Superannuation Act stipulates that a Public Service employee who has reached fifty years of age and has to his credit ten years of pensionable service is entitled to a pension. Parliament should not be guilty of age discrimination
Private Members' Business
towards a group of employees. By reducing their pension, we are punishing these employees and making their situation worse than it is now.

In June 1990 the House of Commons passed Bill C-52, an act to amend the Income Ihx Act and related acts. Regulations made pursuant to the bill clarify in general terms provisions for all Canadians who wish to receive early retirement benefits. Specifically, this bill, C-52, requires that there be no reduction in the amount of early retirement benefit in a registered pension plan if the individual receiving the benefits qualifies in law as pensionable.
I wish to remind this House that the Public Service Superannuation Act does in fact provide for pension benefits for 50-year-old laid off employees with at least 10 years of service, and, as such, these employees are considered to be individuals qualifying in law for early retirement benefits.
In the eighth report of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, tabled June 7, 1990, an agreement was reached between the committee and the Department of Finance regarding modification of the proposed regulations. Concerning early retirement, it was suggested that "there be a provision in the regulations allowing consideration of payment of pensions at an earlier date without actuarial reduction to members who are retiring because of automation, plant closure or downsizing."
Again, in July 1991, the Minister of Finance released draft amendments to the income tax regulations which provided for special benefits for individuals in both the private and public sectors who are terminating employment as a result of a downsizing program that has been approved by the Minister of National Revenue.

Mr. Speaker, I am only going to all this trouble to show how Parliament reacted to the phenomenon of early retirement. I also want to draw your attention to the fact that, even if most provincial civil servants are entitled to early retirement at age 55 without any reduction whatsoever, in some provinces, such as in British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, for example, given specific circumstances and for a limited time, like through a

September 25, 1991
Private Members' Business
down-sizing period, laid-off employees are entitled to early retirement without any reduction.
In Saskatchewan, that applies to laid-off employees as well as civil servants affected outside of Regina. Again, Mr. Speaker, I am pointing out those precedents so that this House recognize the realities Public Service is faced with in the 1990's, when finding how other jurisdictions have solved the matter.
Nobody could anticipate the circumstances we are now in when the Public Service Superannuation Act was first passed by Parliament.

I conclude with the following example of the pension benefits of one of my constituents who was forced to retire because of downsizing in the federal Public Service. This gentleman chose a pension when he was age 50. Consequently, his pension was reduced by 5 per cent a year until the age of 60; that is to say, 5 per cent times 10 years equals a 50 per cent reduction of his total pension.
Had this gentleman been age 55 at the time of lay off he would have received the maximum amount. He wrote to me, and I quote: "My feeling is that the eligible people in this group with at least 10 years service should only have their benefits reduced from the age 55, not 60, as is the current practice. This would mean that I would receive 75 per cent of the maximum amount, instead of the present 50 per cent".
We must act fairly. As a result of the government's policy of downsizing, a segment of its employees are experiencing financial penalty. This can be rectified by acceptance of my motion and amendments to the Public Service Superannuation Act.
I call upon the government to recognize that the act requires amending. This should be accomplished quickly so that when the full effects of Public Service 2000 are felt employees in the 50 to 54 years of age category are not further disadvantaged.

We must act fairly. We must recognize the quality with which public servants discharge their numerous and important tasks. Our attitude in our work relationships with the Public Service will reinforce the benefits of
PS-2000. And we will know that employees having to leave the government between the ages of 50 and 54 will not be further disadvantaged.
