speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the member for Carleton-Gloucester for presenting this Motion M-385. As the New Democratic critic for pensions I fully endorse the proposal put forward by the member.
So we are clear on what we are talking about here, the motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should amend the Public Service Superannuation Act so that any Public Service employee who has lost his or her job on or after January 1st, 1988, as a result of a Public Service downsizing program, and who had reached fifty years of age and had to his or her credit not less than ten years of pensionable service, would be entitled to receive a pension reduced by the product obtained by multiplying:-
The member uses the 5 per cent formula at the age of 55. Downgrading it from the age of 55 to 50 would in fact be treating them the same way as someone reaching the pension at age 60 and downgrading it to 55. I had in my riding a person working for Parks Canada who has experienced the very thing we are discussing.
He is below the age of 55. Parks Canada is downsizing. He was called in and told that he would be eligible for a payout and he would be eligible for his pension rights. He accepted the proposal, took his leave, and waited anxiously for his payout and his pension. After a short period of time he was notified that he did not qualify for the pension and he did not qualify for the payout. He was left completely out.
I have a situation-and this is not a public servant but we are talking about a Crown corporation-in the post office. A senior person, not represented by a union, was six months from the date of receiving her pension, of qualifying for her pension, and Canada Post phased out the post office.
They came in and offered her a buyout. They gave her $16,000 as a buyout. Not even the private sector would have treated this employee that way. It would have carried her for the six months so that she could at least qualify for her pension. They bought her out for $16,000. She then transferred that money into an RRSP figuring that she would have to protect her pension rights.
September 25, 1991

Then she went down to the unemployment insurance office to claim unemployment insurance and found out that she did not qualify for unemployment insurance because she had been bought out. This person not only lost her pension but she lost her unemployment insurance. That is what is happening.
When downsizing is taking place this government must be held responsible. This government must be held responsible for the public servants, and I do not think this bill has gone far enough. I want to say to the member that I support his bill fully.
In my view, in this case because of the 10 years this employee has received there should be no penalty. There should be no penalty whatsoever. The government, being the employer, should be the one who should have to offset that for the five-year period to ensure that the employee receives an equitable pension.
Five years from now when this takes place and the employee reaches the age of 55, the cost of living and the various things which will have taken place will impose a tremendous penalty on this public servant. It will not be his or her fault.
Certainly, he or she is not going to be able to go out. The government says they can transfer their pensions from one area to another. The member has rightly said that at age 50 or above it is very hard to find employment.
The employer has a responsibility either to find another location for that employee to ensure that he or she can reach pensionable age or find a mechanism such as the member has put forward. This change is long overdue and I would urge the government to consider it because of the policies it is bringing in.
I do not agree with some of the changes the Conservatives are talking about with regard to PS 2000 and other programs. For goodness' sake, if they are going to start changing and downsizing then they must take a look at the over-all Superannuation Act and how it affects these employees or bring in some type of training for these people who are let go because of downsizing so that they can carry on in another area.
That is not happening. The sad thing is that we are going to see more and more of this take place. The member's timing is right on. I would urge the govem-

ment to consider this and let this bill come back, be debated and introduced into legislation.
If it does not we are going to be faced with problems for the social programs. Why should we go through this when the people qualified with their 10 years and when they have carried out their duties for that length of time. Many of them might be between the ages of 50 and 55. They are not all 50. We have a period of five years to find some mechanism to ensure that these people are not going to be left out of their pensions because of the actions of the government.
I urge the government to allow this bill to proceed and to encourage this type of mechanism so that employees who have worked for us for many years will receive a decent pension and not be left out, so that they will be able to carry on.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to address the substance of the motion today.
The intentions of the hon. member for Carleton- Gloucester are praiseworthy because the motion's aim is to ensure the financial security of former and present Public Service employees whose employment has or will be lost as a result of downsizing of the Canadian Public Service. As I understand the motion, it proposes that the Public Service Superannuation Act be amended to alter the way in which the pension benefits will be calculated for employees who are at least 50 years of age and have 10 or more years of pensionable service and who have lost their Public Service employment as a result of a layoff or downsizing in their area of work.
For employees in such circumstances, the pension benefits would be calculated by reducing the pension which would be payable at age 55 by 5 per cent for every year that the employee's attained age is less than 55.
I assume first of all that by virtue of the proposed formula anyone whose employment has been terminated under these circumstances and who has already reached 55 years of age would not have any reduction in pension. Basically, this is what happens now under the existing terms of the Public Service Superannuation Act, although Treasury Board approval is required in each case.

September 25, 1991
Private Members' Business
There is, however, one difference between the existing superannuation legislation and the proposal in the motion, and that is with respect to the service requirements which an employee needs to qualify for the benefit.
Under the present law, to qualify for a waiver of pension reduction an employee must be at least age 55 and have 10 or more years of employment in the Public Service. Under the motion this requirement reads 10 years of pensionable service.
Pensionable service under the Public Service Superannuation Act is made up of a variety of kinds of service, not all which needs to be with the Public Service of Canada. If, for example, an employee has imported pension credits from an outside employer, under the terms of a reciprocal pension transfer agreement those pension credits are considered to be pensionable service.
Under the proposed amendment being discussed today, as the motion is worded a person could have 10 years of pensionable service and qualify for an unreduced pension, even though almost none of it was employment in the Public Service of Canada.
To use another example, the Public Service Superannuation Act does not yet permit the accounting of service where an employee regularly works fewer than 30 hours per week. An employee could have worked in the Public Service for 10 years but, if some of that employment was on a part-time basis, he or she would not qualify for the benefits under the proposed wording of the motion today.
I would therefore argue that in the terms of qualifying for special treatment on layoff or downsizing, the existing criterion of requiring 10 years of employment rather than 10 years of pensionable service is fair since it recognizes actual employment in the Public Service, either full or part-time, as opposed to pension credits which can be transferred to the superannuation plan from an outside employer.
The proposal's application to employees over age 55 seems relatively straightforward. However, in the case of employees between ages 50 and 55, it is not completely clear to me how the proposal is intended to operate. The motion proposes that eligible employees receive a pension reduced by multiplying the number of years that the employee is less than age 55 by 5 per cent of the amount of the pension that would have been payable if the
employee had been 55 years of age at the time of the loss of his or her job.
Does the hon. member, in referring to the pension that would have been payable if the employee had been 55 years of age, mean a reduced or an unreduced pension? Under the Public Service Superannuation Act, at age 55 only those public servants with 30 or more years of pensionable service would be entitled to draw an unreduced pension.
Employees at age 55 with fewer than 30 years service would be entitled to a reduced pension. For example, if an employee was laid off at age 52 with 26 years of service, under the existing law he or she would be able to receive an immediate annual allowance reduced by 20 per cent. Under the formula proposed in the motion, because of the way the PSSA operates the same individual at age 55 would still have a 20 per cent reduction. The motion would require that this reduced pension would be further reduced by 15 per cent because the employee is three years younger than age 55.
It is possible that the hon. member means to propose that in the above example we are to assume that the employee would also have three more years of pensionable service by age 55, in which case his or her pension would under the existing terms of the Public Service Superannuation Act be reduced by only 5 per cent.
If we were to take this 95 per cent pension and reduce it further by 15 per cent as proposed under the formula set out in the motion, we end up with a pension benefit very close to an amount which is provided under the existing arrangement under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
The employee in this example would receive 81.5 per cent of his or her unreduced pension under the proposed formula instead of 80 per cent under the present terms of the Public Service Superannuation Act.
For the employee who does not have more than 25 years of service at the time of the layoff, the situation is marginally better. At age 52, with 15 years of service, an employee's reduction under the existing Public Service Superannuation Act would be 40 per cent. This means a 60 per cent pension would be payable. By age 55, the reduction would be only 25 per cent. Under the proposed amendment that 75 per cent pension would then be reduced by a further 15 per cent so that the employee
September 25, 1991

would receive 64.5 per cent of his or her unreduced pension.
This example, as in the earlier one, is not clear whether the hon. member proposing the motion intends that service be imputed to employees covered when he refers to the pension that would have been payable if the employee had been 55. If that is the case, then the proposal becomes costly and would in fact be unacceptable under the newly revised income tax provisions and the regulations governing tax assisted retirement savings.
Under a defined benefit pension plan such as the Public Service Superannuation Act, pension credit cannot be given for service which does not actually take place. If the hon. member is assuming that at age 55 all Public Service pensions should be unreduced, we would be looking at an extremely costly proposal since it would be in effect lowering the retirement age under the pension plan. Such a proposal would be so far out of line with private sector practice as to be unacceptable.
Turning to the retroactive nature of the proposed motion, it would be quite unusual to provide pension improvements on a retroactive basis at all, much less to cover a period of almost four years. Prospective pension changes are the norm because of the liabilities associated with such improvements as well as the administrative complexities of recalculating benefits and making retroactive adjustments in the case of the active pensioner and the survivors of any who have died.
In conclusion, I must report to the House that the motion is technically flawed and its exact application is not immediately clear. If it is to improve pension arrangements for persons laid off between the age of 50 and 55, it needs to be recast to accomplish the objective. Nevertheless, it is the case that the existing pension arrangements are already relatively generous and although they favour the older worker, that is so because of the difficulties older workers face obtaining other employment after being laid off from the Public Service.
In the case of somewhat younger workers, the reduced pension is available to supplement their incomes in the event that subsequent employment is not obtained at a comparable salary to their Public Service earnings.
Private Members' Business
Public Service pensions are, as members know, indexed to the cost of living.
Hon. members may also wish to bear in mind that the public servants receive severance and other benefits under the work force adjustment policy so that they are treated fairly in relation to their private sector counterparts who find themselves in similar circumstances.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to commend the hon. member for Carleton- Gloucester for bringing this matter to the attention of the House and for the proposal he has put forward in regard to this matter and also for the example of the employee with the parks service.
However, before the government would table such a bill I would submit that the proposal would have to be explained thoroughly. I am sure that the President of the Treasury Board would want to have the views of his advisory committee on the matter.
Quite apart from the specific proposal that is in front of us, I think that this House should consider the merits or otherwise of proceeding with a single change to the pension plan for public service in advance of a comprehensive public sector pension reform package. I believe the whole matter should be looked at. I am sure individuals would agree that if there is a change made in this particular area it may impact in another area we are not completely aware of and perhaps provide a penalty to some other individual.
I believe that members are well aware that work has gone on for some considerable time on changes to the federal Public Service statutory pension plans. In fact, I understand that the President of the Treasury Board hopes to be presenting a reform package to the House in the near future.
The impetus for reform, in fact the need for reform, comes from a number of sources. For example, in the various studies which followed the coming into force of section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms there were a few areas where the government made a commitment to consider the matter in the context of pension reform.

Private Members' Business
While some of these matters were dealt with in the so-called "remarriage bill" which was enacted by this Parliament in June 1989, there are still a few matters needing attention in the whole area of pension reform.
While I am not sure that this is a strict section 15 issue, one of the items which stems from the Equality for All report of the parliamentary committee on equality rights is the problem of providing for the division of pension credits on marriage breakdown. This is one particular area about which I am sure many members of this House have also had constituents come in and make complaints or ask for reforms to be made.
Under the current statutes there is no provision to pay pension benefits to anyone other than the plan member or the member's surviving dependants except in response to a court order for family maintenance. This last order is provided for under the Garnishment and Pension Diversion Act which is limited to situations where the non-member spouse is entitled to maintenance under a court order.
The Garnishment and Pension Diversion Act does not apply to situations where property, that is family assets, are being divided. I am sure many members have received representations, as I have mentioned, from former spouses of public servants that the pension plan should be amended to accommodate court order division of pensions as part of an equalization of family assets on marriage breakdown. Obviously this is a matter that should be looked at.
Another very important pressure for pension reform is the Income Tax Act where recent changes instituted a fair set of rules for tax relief granted in respect of contributions to pension plans. The Income Tax Act and its regulations now set out the maximum benefits that a pension plan can provide and still have a registered status. Only contributions to a registered pension plan are tax deductible. We recognize that employers may want to make income arrangements for retired employees that exceed the registered pension plan limits, but the tax act does provide for retirement compensation arrangements.
The tax treatment of retirement compensation arrangements is different from the treatment of registered pension plans.
I really do not want to go much further into the new tax rules for retirement savings. However, I do want to
emphasize that there is a new system which all private pension plans must adhere to. I think that members will agree that it is important that federal Public Service pension plans be structured in compliance with the current Income Tax Act requirements.
Yet another pressure for reform of federal public sector plans is recognition of the requirements of the Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985.
The statute which was enacted applies to all pensions provided by an employer engaged in a federal undertaking. However, it specifically does not apply in respect of pension plans related to employment in right of Canada.
While the Income Tax Act, because it has to do with a fair allocation of the tax burden, is concerned with the maximum benefits a pension plan can provide, the focus of the Pension Benefits Standards Act has more to do with the protection of persons who are members of pension plans. The carrying out of this protection is done by regulating a wide range of matters, including funding and investment, the trust nature of pension funds, plan members' rights to information, joint employee-employer committees, protection of plan members in cases of sales, acquisitions and mergers, and a prohibition against retroactive reduction in accrued benefits.
The Pension Benefits Standards Act of 1985 also sets out minimum requirements in terms of what a pension plan is to provide. These minimum requirements extend to matters such as maximum waiting periods for membership, coverage of part-time employees, two-year vesting and lock-in, that is the right to a pension benefit, maximum rate of interest on refunds of contributions, guaranteed portability options, access to a pension upon early retirement, and minimum pre-retirement and post-retirement survivor benefits.
As hon. members know, the public sector pension plans are good, solid and fair plans. However, while the plans do exceed certain of the minimum requirements of the Pension Benefits Standards Act, there are some of the requirements which are not met.
Pension reform should address any non-compliance with these requirements which are imposed on private pension plans in the federal sector. The foregoing relates more or less to the external pressures for pension reform. I think hon. members are also well aware of the many internal pressures for action, including, of course,
September 25, 1991

an early retirement program for correctional service employees.
The point I wanted to make by this survey of the pressures for reform is that it does not seem prudent or efficient to move on a single issue in advance of a major reform package. In terms of the thrust of the motion itself, both the Income Tax Act and the regulations and the Pension Benefits Standards Act have something to say about early retirement. It is obvious that any change should be assessed in the context of parliamentary directions to private pension plans.
There is a broader issue too, namely, the possibility of constraining any future redesign of the pension plan which would take into account all of the reform pressures.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I think it is premature to consider this motion on the eve of the presentation of a total pension reform package, and the items I mentioned should be considered in this entire package.
Again, it is noteworthy that the member has brought this particular matter forward. We have had examples cited to us. There is obviously something that should be done with regard to Public Service pension plans in these matters, but it should be done in the context of a total reform package. I am sure the hon. member will be pushing the President of the Treasury Board to put that reform package in front of Parliament just as soon as possible.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:
In following up on the comments of my colleague who just finished speaking, I am certain the hon. member from Carleton-Gloucester will be pushing Treasury Board for changes. I am sure there are many of us who will be also standing with him to encourage some of those changes. I would like to commend him for his interest, his compassion and his feeling for the employees of the federal government. I think it is commendable and it is something that we all are interested in.
I had the opportunity this summer to meet with members of the superannuates association in Red Deer. They outlined to me the history of negotiations they have had with Treasury Board, some of the concerns that they have been expressing to different governments over many, many years. They have a lot of concerns they are hoping will be addressed at the same time.
Private Members' Business
I would like today to comment on the motion before us in the context of the already generous early retirement provisions in the Public Service Superannuation Act. While the government and each one of us here recognizes that there is always room for change and improvement in any scheme, the existing early retirement arrangements under the act already go a long way toward meeting the needs of Public Service employees.
The Treasury Board as the employer is apparently satisfied that when older workers must leave the Public Service work force before reaching retirement age, they have adequate and fair pensions and some flexibility in their pension options. Mr. Speaker, you know as I do that Treasury Board has the responsibility to evaluate employee benefit programs, to ensure that the employees are fairly recompensed and that their benefit plans are adequate.
We as members also have a responsibility to government employees and we have to balance that responsibility with another one that we have to the Canadian taxpayer. We have also got a responsibility to those superannuates who are already on pension and no longer working for the government.
As has been mentioned, the present plan is under scrutiny. It is also under scrutiny by the private sector. Many of them are looking at it jealously. In comparison to many of them, it is a generous program.
For the benefits of the members of this House who are not aware of some of the current conditions, I would like to briefly go through the retirement benefits that are in place now and available to public servants under the existing pension plan.
To begin with, public servants' normal pensionable age is 60. Thus, any public servant who has at least five years of pensionable service and has reached age 60 is entitled to an immediate pension. This pension will be calculated on the basis of 2 per cent of the plan member's average salary over his or her highest six consecutive years of service.
For those members in the House who are listening and notice, I should perhaps expand on that. The individual who has worked for only five years, I am told, will have his pension based on the average of the total service, not

September 25, 1991
Private Members' Business
on six years, because of course they did not have enough service for that.
The typical employee though does not start work for the federal government at age 55. Many, many start much younger. The Public Service Superannuation Act contains special early retirement provisions for employees who have reached at least age 55 and have 30 or more years of pensionable service. These people may retire on an unreduced pension. It is a pension based on the same formula as I just described for normal retirement; that is, 2 per cent per year of the average salary times years of service.
There has been much talk about retirement age in the last few years. I should comment that for pension plans age 65 is still the most widely accepted normal retirement age under employee sponsored pension plans in Canada. According to the 1988 StatsCanada study of pension plans in our country, 90 per cent of all pension plans covering 80 per cent of the total membership in those plans still provide for normal retirement at age 65.
I should like to point out as well that not only does the Public Service Superannuation Act provide for a relatively earlier normal retirement age, but it also provides for relatively earlier special retirement provisions. Special early retirement provisions exist in only a small percentage of Canadian pension plans. Where they do, age 60 is the most frequent age of entitlement and 30 years of service is the most common minimum period.
In terms of early retirement provisions, that is, provisions for reduced pensions in situations where employees leave the workforce before having reached age 60 or age 55 with 30 or more years of service, the Public Service Superannuation Act provides two benefit formulae for calculating pensions. The formula used depends upon the pensionable service credit which an individual has to his or her credit on retirement and the contributor's age.
The normal retirement formula for any plan member who has reached age 50 is to reduce the pension which would be payable at retirement age. For those in the business of employee benefits, this reduction is normally called a deferred annuity. It is 5 per cent per year for each year that the employee's age is less than 60 years. At age 55 an individual's pension would be reduced by 25
per cent, that is the age difference of five years multiplied by 5 per cent to equal 25 per cent.
Using this formula at age 50 the individual's deferred annuity would be reduced by 50 per cent. This formula roughly equates to an actuarial reduction. Such a reduction takes into account the fact that a retirement pension which begins to be paid earlier than at normal retirement is paid over a longer period of time. Accordingly, it should be reduced to take into account that longer period of time over which the payments are spread as compared to the payment period for a pension which is deferred until the plan member reaches retirement age.
Actuarial reduction is quite a mouthful. It simply means, as they have said here, that they anticipate or expect that everybody is going to live to a certain age and should you retire early, they are going to reduce your pension by an amount so that you will collect approximately the same amount of money should you live to be the same age as the average Canadian.
There is a second formula in the Public Service Superannuates Act which gives an advantage to employees with long service. Long service is recognized in employees who have 25 or more years of service and have reached age 50. In those circumstances, a pension would be reduced by the greater of 5 per cent for each year that the employee's age is less than 55, or 5 per cent for each year that the employee's pensionable service credit is less than 30.
For example, an employee aged 52, with 29 years of service would receive a pension equal to his or her deferred annuity reduced by 15 per cent. That is the greater of the reduction done by age, because 55 minus 52 is 3 times 5 per cent, which would equal a 15 per cent reduction.
Of course for the person with 30 years of service minus 29, which would have been a 5 per cent reduction, because it was the greater, it is reduced by 15.
Under this same formula an employee aged 50 or more who leaves the workforce with 25 or more years of pensionable service would have a maximum reduction of 25 per cent. In other words, the employee would receive 75 per cent of his or her deferred annuity. This compares, of course, to the person without the long service
September 25, 1991

award who would in the same situation see his pension reduced by 50 per cent.
There is, as some hon. members might know, one more special retirement provision which completes the retirement package for Public Service employees. I refer to the provision whereby the Treasury Board can waive the early retirement reduction or penalty, as it is sometimes called. The Public Service Superannuation Act sets out those conditions. The employee must have reached age 55, must have at least 10 years employment in the Public Service and must retire on an involuntary basis. Since this provision was introduced in 1971, it has been applied in many individual cases of layoff or where a Public Service employee's position has been declared redundant.
However, in recent years the Treasury Board has gone further and has given pre-approval in principle to the waiver of pension reduction in any case where an employee has been declared surplus under the terms of the Public Service Workforce Adjustment Policy.
This means that eligible older workers who lose their employment through workforce adjustments or downsizing exercises will not actually have their pensions reduced, even thought they have not reached age 60 or met the 55 with 30 years service thresholds.
I might finally add that all early and special retirement pensions are indexed under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act from the year following the year leaving employment. This immediate indexing provides an invaluable measure of security for employees who leave the workforce in advance of reaching retirement age.
As I said earlier, it is an easy matter to devise better pension arrangements. The difficulty lies in paying for them. Among the most costly of pension improvements is lowering the age at which unreduced pensions are paid. Given the already generous pensionable ages under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the fact that the proposal we are debating would fall into the category of the more expensive kind of improvement, it is difficult for me to support today's motion. Even though it would apply to a relatively small segment of the Public Service pension population, it would still be viewed as excessive by members of the private sector workforce, many of whom have either no pension coverage at all or have less comprehensive coverage. I believe
Private Members' Business
that our Public Service pension arrangements must be kept in line with those of other Canadian employers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE MOTION TO AMEND THE PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a significant part of the discussion that is going on here this evening is rather dry and boring. It is unfortunate that it is hard to liven up a debate such as this. I do appreciate the efforts of all of those involved in the debate this evening, but once again, it is pretty hard to liven up some of the cold figures that are brought forward.
I know I have limited time and I have quite a prepared presentation to make this evening. It is my hope that if this debate is renewed that those involved with the debate will inform me so that I can come before the House and possibly continue the presentation if I am not able to complete it this evening. It is unfortunate that when the speaker's list was put up there was not a little more consideration with respect to the information of which I am in possession of. There is a little bit more history, and quite possibly by presenting the history preceding the other debate it would be more valuable to those with us this evening.
The Public Service Superannuation Act covers approximately 308,000 Public Service employees and sets out the terms of their pension coverage. At the present time, full unreduced pensions are payable under the act when a plan member reaches age 60 with at least five years of pensionable service to his credit, or at age 55 with 30 years of pensionable service, or at any age if retirement is due to disability, provided that the person has completed at least five years of pensionable service.
The act also provides reduced early retirement pensions, known as annual allowances. This means that any plan member with at lest five years of pensionable service can retire as early as age 50 and immediately start to receive a pension. However, the pension that is payable is reduced by 5 per cent for each year that the plan member is less than the age of 60, which means that the maximum reduction is 50 per cent.
This reduction is made and is indeed necessary under the costing arrangements of the act to reflect the longer period over which that early pension will be payable. The reduction for plan members who retire at age 50 or with 25 or more years of pensionable service is related either to age 55 or to 30 years of pensionable service, rather

Private Members' Business
than age 60. The maximum reduction possible is 25 per cent, rather than 50 per cent.
In cases of layoffs the Treasury Board may waive the reduction provided the plan member is at least age 55 and has a minimum of 10 years pensionable service to his credit. This provision was introduced by way of an amendment to the act in 1971 and was rendered more generous by a Treasury Board decision of July 1987 that makes the waiver of reduction more or less automatic where employment is lost due to downsizing.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester would mean that in such cases an annual allowance would be payable up to five years earlier than it is at the moment. As well, although the potential maximum reduction of 25 per cent would remain the same, logic would dictate that the existing waiver of reduction policy should be extended to cover the new arrangement.
The consequent payment of a pension over a longer period of time starting at age 50 rather than at age 55 would result in increased cost with the size of that increase directly related to the number of pensions being paid out under these circumstances. These are costs which would have to be paid for by active plan members and the government, as the employer, and could result in increased contributions. With their contribution already equal to 7.5 per cent of their salary, any increase, however small, might not be well received by plan members.
I would just like to remind the Elouse that a change in design, which this proposal is, would be more effectively achieved by the Public Service pension plan reform process than through an amendment to the act since the government has indicated its intentions to introduce a Public Service pension reform bill this autumn. Until this bill is tabled, any impact it may have on the early retirement features of the current plan cannot be assessed. I will, however, remind hon. members that a previous Public Service pension reform initiative, Bill C-33, which died on the Order Paper when the last federal election was called, would have brought considerable changes to the Public Service pension arrangements.
This is not the appropriate time to describe all the proposed changes, but I would like to indicate that the financial and accounting side of the plan would have been revised to observe more closely the requirements and constraints imposed by the government on other employers and to enhance the financial security of the Public Service arrangements.
The cost for post reform service would have been shared equally between the government, as employer, and plan members with benefits being fully funded as they were earned.
A joint employer plan member Pension Management Board would have been established for the Public Service to permit any plan member involvement in the operation of the pension plan and to reflect the equal cost and risk sharing of the new arrangements.
The Pension Management Board would have significant input on the plan design. It was to have six months from its appointment to report to the President of the Treasury Board on its recommendations for the changes to be made to the Public Service pension plan to bring it into line with the standards and practices required of other employer sponsored pension plans.
